lessons.drill: Have a colleague ask you a hard, open question on camera or with a stopwatch running. Score it two ways: time from their last word to your first word, and whether you spoke again before they finished an extended answer. Good performance: at least five seconds of silence before you respond, and zero interruptions of their elaboration. Anything under three seconds, or any interruption, is a fail and worth reviewing on tape.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: AI Slowdown Fears Jolt Markets, Oil Spikes
blocks.script:
Good morning. Markets are digesting a wave of unsettling headlines from artificial intelligence to oil supply disruptions, all while central bankers prepare for a pivotal week of interest rate decisions.

Let's start with the story rattling tech investors. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an open letter over the weekend calling for a global slowdown in AI development, according to reporting cited in The Peak. Amodei warned that AI systems are now advancing so quickly, partly because they're helping build the next generation of AI, that the technology risks outrunning humanity's ability to understand and control it. He committed Anthropic to slowing down unilaterally and promised outside evaluators permanent access to check on safety measures.

OpenAI's Sam Altman and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis both backed the call, with Altman also saying he's pushing OpenAI's planned public listing back to at least 2027, calling this an unwise moment to go public. But not everyone is convinced this is purely about safety. The White House's AI point man, David Sacks, described the move as a bid for regulatory capture. Cohere's CEO Aidan Gomez went further, according to the Globe and Mail, accusing the industry of essentially coordinating cartel-like behavior. President Trump, meanwhile, has been dismissing the safety warnings as something close to a conspiracy against the technology.

Wall Street didn't take the news well. Bloomberg's Markets Daily reported steep declines across AI-linked names, with Japan's Softbank down eleven percent given its massive stake in OpenAI. Chipmakers took a beating too. South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung both fell sharply, and in Europe, ASML dropped more than four percent while France's Soitec plunged twelve percent. In the U.S., Nvidia and memory makers like Micron and Western Digital were also under pressure in premarket trading. Interestingly, software companies seen as less exposed to an AI slowdown, like Adobe, Salesforce and Crowdstrike, actually gained ground.

At the same time, oil markets are on edge after Saudi Arabia was forced to shut down a major crude pipeline following attacks, according to Reuters reporting cited across the newsletters. Traders say as much as four percent of global oil supply could be affected. That's on top of ongoing disruptions tied to the Strait of Hormuz, meaning roughly a fifth of the world's oil is now caught up in geopolitical turmoil. Brent crude jumped more than two percent in the wake of the news, and diplomatic talks on a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz have reportedly been postponed.

There's also a diesel angle here. President Trump has asked Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries, arguing the attacks are worsening a global diesel shortage. U.S. diesel prices reportedly hit a record high above six dollars a gallon on average last week, an unwelcome development for the White House heading into midterm elections in November.

All of this is landing in a market already nervous about interest rates. Central banks in the United States, United Kingdom and Japan all have decisions this week, starting with the Federal Reserve on Wednesday. According to Bloomberg, JPMorgan's chief U.S. economist now expects the Fed to hike rates twice this year, in September and December, a notable shift given President Trump has repeatedly pushed for lower borrowing costs. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh appears to have little room to maneuver, with underlying inflation not cooling fast enough to justify holding steady. The Globe and Mail notes this sets up a direct clash between Warsh and the president. With the ten-year Treasury yield hovering just below five percent, some investors argue the Fed is already behind the curve.

Here in Canada, inflation data released Monday showed the headline consumer price index holding steady at three percent in August, unchanged from July, according to the Globe and Mail's coverage of Statistics Canada figures. Gasoline prices actually eased slightly during the month, but were still about twenty-three percent higher than a year earlier. Grocery inflation has cooled somewhat but continues to outpace overall inflation, squeezing lower-income households the hardest. Core measures the Bank of Canada watches closely remain closer to two percent, and most economists expect the central bank to hold rates again at its next decision in late October, though Governor Tiff Macklem has signaled he'd consider hiking if energy costs spill over into broader prices.

Canada's housing market is also showing strain. Data from the Canadian Real Estate Association showed home sales fell nearly seven percent in August, even as the national average sale price ticked up slightly to just over six hundred sixty-eight thousand dollars, according to the Globe and Mail.

On the investment front, Prime Minister Mark Carney kicked off his high-profile Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, drawing what Bloomberg described as money managers overseeing more than seventy trillion dollars in assets. The goal is to generate a trillion dollars in investment over five years for major projects, with officials pointing to more than one hundred sixty projects open for funding, including a proposed high-speed rail link between Edmonton and Calgary and a large expansion of the Port of Churchill.

There was already momentum heading into the summit. TD Bank committed one hundred fifty billion dollars to fund Canadian companies in critical sectors over the next five years, while Scotiabank pledged one hundred billion dollars, according to the Globe and Mail. Reports also indicate Brookfield and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board are preparing to launch a fifty billion dollar fund aimed at strategic sectors. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said she expects concrete deal announcements to come out of the gathering.

Still, questions remain about whether enthusiasm will translate into signed deals. Capital Power's CEO reportedly told the Globe and Mail that removing regulatory roadblocks will be the real test in turning investor interest into final investment decisions.

On trade, President Trump told reporters over the weekend that a deal with Canada could come fairly soon, downplaying talk of the U.S. walking away from the North American trade agreement. Carney echoed that optimism last week, saying he doesn't expect further tariff retaliation from either side.

Elsewhere in politics, exit polls showed Sweden's centre-left bloc winning its parliamentary election with a combined fifty-one percent of the vote, according to Reuters, bucking the rightward trend seen elsewhere in Europe and delivering a surprisingly weak result for the Sweden Democrats.

Finally, on the market snapshot from Monday: the TSX, S&P 500, Dow and Nasdaq were all higher, gold ticked up slightly, but oil fell on the day even as later reporting pointed to renewed spikes tied to the Saudi pipeline situation. The Canadian dollar weakened against its U.S. counterpart, trading around seventy-two cents U.S.
talkingPoints: One, AI industry leaders including Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman are calling for a coordinated slowdown in development, citing safety risks, though critics call it a bid to shape regulation in their favor.
Two, the AI slowdown talk triggered a global selloff in tech and chip stocks, from Japan's Softbank to Nvidia, while software firms seen as less exposed gained.
Three, Saudi Arabia's shutdown of a major oil pipeline after attacks has traders bracing for a possible four percent hit to global crude supply, pushing oil prices higher.

Four, the Federal Reserve, Bank of England and Bank of Japan all face pivotal rate decisions this week, with markets increasingly betting on a Fed hike that could put Chair Kevin Warsh at odds with President Trump.

Five, Canadian inflation held steady at three percent in August, while Prime Minister Carney's Investment Summit in Toronto has already produced major funding pledges from TD, Scotiabank, Brookfield and CPPIB.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: AI Slowdown Fears Rattle Global Markets
blocks.script:
Good evening. Tonight's top story: the world's biggest artificial intelligence companies are calling for a slower pace of development, and markets are reacting with unease.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei published an open letter over the weekend warning that AI is now being used to build the next generation of AI, a process he called recursive self-improvement. He said this summer saw progress accelerating so fast that it risks outrunning humanity's ability to understand and control these systems. Amodei committed Anthropic to slowing down on its own and giving independent evaluators deep access to check its safety work.

OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk all echoed the call. Altman also said OpenAI's planned stock market listing will be pushed back to at least 2027.

Not everyone is convinced this is about safety. White House AI adviser David Sacks suggested it may be a bid for regulatory capture, and Cohere's chief executive Aidan Gomez, speaking to the Globe and Mail, called coordinated slowdown talk cartel behaviour. President Donald Trump dismissed fears of an AI takeover as a hoax, insisting the only guardrail AI needs is a strong president.

The debate hit markets hard. Tech and chip stocks led a global selloff, with Nvidia, memory chip makers and SoftBank all sliding. At the same time, the yield on the 10-year US Treasury note pushed above 5 percent for the first time since 2023, adding pressure on stretched equity valuations. Analysts at Standard Bank now see that yield climbing further, toward the low 5 percent range by year end.

Feeding the anxiety is a surge in oil prices after Saudi Arabia was forced to shut a major crude pipeline following drone and Houthi attacks in the Red Sea, with traders warning as much as 4 percent of global oil supply could be affected. That combines with ongoing disruption at the Strait of Hormuz.

All of this sets up a pivotal week for central banks. The US Federal Reserve, under new chair Kevin Warsh, is widely expected to raise interest rates on Wednesday despite pressure from President Trump to cut, followed by decisions in Britain and Japan.

In Canada, Prime Minister Mark Carney's first Investment Summit is under way in Toronto, drawing money managers overseeing more than 70 trillion dollars. Bell Canada, TD, Scotiabank, Brookfield and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board have all announced billions in new commitments to energy, AI infrastructure and critical minerals.

And in central Africa, health officials say Ebola continues to spread in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with more than 7,000 confirmed cases and over 3,000 deaths, after a newly diagnosed patient travelled roughly 2,500 kilometres through three countries while infectious.

blocks.label: Practice: Tax, Regulatory & Industry
blocks.title: Insurance Churn, CCPC Passive Income, and Bank Billions
blocks.script:
Start with the number that should worry every advisor in this business: life insurers are losing clients at a rate that Wealth Professional is calling alarming, based on new global research into consumer engagement. The finding isn't that people don't want coverage, it's that they don't understand what they own or why they own it, and they lapse policies rather than call anyone to ask. That's a service gap you can close. If you have clients with permanent policies bought a decade or more ago, this is the week to call and walk through what the policy actually does, especially before year end conversations about corporate owned insurance for incorporated business owners.

On the regulatory side, CIRO has permanently banned a former TD representative after a hearing panel found he misappropriated roughly 150,000 dollars in client transfers. The panel ordered 350,000 dollars in fines and disgorgement. Separately, the Manitoba Securities Commission has now assigned its investment dealer and mutual fund dealer registration function to CIRO, part of a national push by the Canadian Securities Administrators to centralize registration and cut duplication for firms operating across provinces. If you're dually registered, expect your compliance department to mention this soon.

Now the one that actually changes advice today: Canadian controlled private corporation passive income rules. The small business deduction on active income starts grinding down once a corporation's adjusted aggregate investment income passes 50,000 dollars in the prior year, and the deduction disappears entirely at 150,000. That's five dollars of small business limit lost for every dollar of passive income above the threshold. For physicians and other incorporated professionals sitting on retained earnings inside a professional corporation, this is the conversation to have before December: are they parking too much cash and too many marketable securities inside the corp, and would an insurance funded strategy, a corporate class structure, or simply cleaner dividend timing keep more of that active income taxed at the roughly 12 percent small business rate instead of the general rate near 26 and a half.

On the family side, Globe Advisor's look at high net worth RESP planning is worth passing to clients with young kids. Registered education savings plans were deferring tax on 98.6 billion dollars in assets nationally at the end of last year, and wealthy families carry meaningfully higher balances. The debate isn't whether to fund one, it's contribution pacing and how withdrawals get structured to avoid dumping too much taxable growth on a student in one year.

Speaking of family money flowing the wrong direction, RBC's new poll finds one in five parents are still financially supporting adult children between 35 and 40. That's not a rounding error, that's a full generation of parents delaying their own retirement drawdown. If you have pre retirees who keep topping up a grown child, put a number on it this quarter, because it's probably larger than they're telling you.

The Fraser Institute is out with research suggesting government spending may be crowding out charitable giving. Ottawa's social benefit outlays have roughly doubled since 1961, while the share of Canadians donating to registered charities has fallen by close to a third. For clients doing estate planning, this is useful context when you raise donor advised funds or charitable remainder trusts. Fewer Canadians are giving, which means the ones who still do carry more weight, and there's a case for structuring that giving to actually count for something rather than writing a cheque in December.

Underneath all of this, financial insecurity is rising broadly. New national data shows close to half of working Canadians feel worse off than a year ago, and it's not concentrated at the bottom, women and parents in particular report thinner safety nets regardless of income level. That's a prompt to revisit emergency fund targets even with your higher income households.

On product and fees, Wealth Professional flags a Northern Trust survey of 300 global investment leaders showing asset managers are curbing new product launches and leaning on outsourcing and AI to run leaner shops. Pair that with private equity fundraising rebounding even as exits stay slow, testing limited partner patience on holding periods. And a good explainer piece this week traces how exchange traded funds opened global markets to Canadian retail investors in the first place. All three point the same direction: fewer flashy new launches, more consolidation into low cost, liquid wrappers.

On the macro backdrop, Canada's banks and pension funds are putting real money behind Carney's investment summit in Toronto. BMO pledged up to 70 billion dollars over ten years, TD committed 150 billion over five, Scotiabank launched a new growth institute with 100 billion, and CIBC earmarked 2 billion specifically for small and medium defence firms. Ontario Teachers' says it'll add another 10 billion to its Canadian book by 2027. Combined infrastructure pledges now sit near 85 billion dollars against a municipal infrastructure gap estimated at 240 billion.

South of the border, sticky inflation has pushed odds of a Federal Reserve hike this week to 85 percent, with supercore inflation up half a point on the month. The Bank of Canada is on the watch list here too: it holds at its next decision October 28, and Governor Macklem has said he'd consider hiking only if energy costs spill into broader prices. Don't reposition fixed income books on Fed noise alone.

Two more worth a mention. The Globe reports aspiring doctors are increasingly training abroad at far higher cost after being shut out of competitive Canadian admissions, racking up six figure debt before they've billed a single hour. If you have young physician clients in this position, loan structuring and disability insurance timing matter more than usual. And the Canada Child Benefit's September payment landed a few days early this cycle, worth a one line heads up to clients who budget around it.
talkingPoints: Call clients holding old permanent life policies before year end, most don't know what they actually own.
If a professional corporation cleared 50,000 in passive income last year, its small business deduction is already shrinking.
Ask pre retiree clients what they're really spending supporting adult kids, then put a real number on it.
Charitable giving is falling nationally, so structure what your donor clients still give to make it count.
Bank of Canada holds October 28, don't let Fed rate noise this week drive Canadian portfolio changes.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Churchill Costs, Sex-Ed Overhaul, Mayoral Race Heats Up
blocks.script:
Start with the number that matters most for anyone watching Manitoba's northern trade push. Premier Wab Kinew has been telling investors in Toronto that a Port of Churchill expansion could run as high as 80 billion dollars. But CBC reports that Arctic Gateway Group, the company that actually owns the port and the Hudson Bay Railway, says it only needs a fraction of that, less than 3 billion dollars, to upgrade the port and the rail line connecting it to the rest of the country. Arctic Gateway is a partnership of 29 First Nations and remote communities. Combined federal and provincial funding to date sits around 262 million dollars, nowhere near the headline figure the premier is pitching. On top of that, Manitoba is now offering a provincial sales tax exemption on major capital investment tied to the Churchill project, part of the province's push to woo investors at the Canada Investment Summit. If you have clients weighing exposure to Manitoba infrastructure plays, the gap between the premier's number and the operator's number is worth flagging directly.

On education, Manitoba's first real sex-ed overhaul in about 25 years is now in front of more than 100 pilot schools. The Free Press reports the new health curriculum weaves lessons on consent and the menstrual cycle into every grade from kindergarten through grade 12, instead of concentrating them at a few checkpoints. Grade 7 students are now working through the specific conditions of consent, freely given, reversible, informed, enthusiastic, and specific. A mandatory rollout across the province is set for the 2028-29 school year. Expect this to come up at dinner tables and school board meetings alike this fall.

Winnipeg's municipal election campaign got its first real test yesterday. Mayoral candidates held their first all-candidates debate of the 2026 race, and transit dominated it. CBC reports candidates criticized attacks on bus drivers and promised service improvements. Separately, candidate Don Woodstock is promising to hire more firefighters and paramedics, funded by cutting overtime costs, as part of a broader plan to overhaul how the city manages emergency services. With the vote weeks away, watch for more spending promises like this one.

Health care is generating uncomfortable questions again. A Winnipeg family says a critical incident review into the death of Stacey Ross, who died following a long wait at St. Boniface Hospital, has left them without real closure. That's going to keep coming up as a pressure point on the health authority heading into the fall.

Away from the city, the Swan River Valley is still digging out. That region was hit by flooding twice this summer, and CBC reports rebuilding is underway with residents facing costly repairs and lingering trauma, all while local governments try to balance disaster response with October's municipal election. It's a reminder that flood risk in rural Manitoba isn't a one-off story this year.

There's also a troubling follow-up out of East St. Paul. A 5.5 million dollar daycare, built two years ago with provincial funding, now sits derelict, vacant, stripped by scavengers and damaged by flooding. That's public money that never delivered a single childcare space, and it's the kind of story that raises real questions about provincial project oversight.

A few quicker items you'll want on your radar. Environment Canada and the province issued a wind alert for central and southern Manitoba, with gusts forecast up to 95 kilometres an hour early Tuesday, so expect possible power and travel disruptions. Zebra mussel larvae have now been confirmed in Lake Winnipegosis and Waterhen Lake, triggering a provincial aquatic invasive species response and mandatory watercraft decontamination for anyone using those lakes. Winnipeg police say officers involved in Friday's West Broadway pursuit, which left a person seriously injured, were responding to a possible abduction call. And a 21-year-old man was killed in an animal attack on a western Manitoba First Nation last week. The province has ruled out a bear, and the exact animal is still unconfirmed.

On the highway safety file, a Manitoba man who lost his daughter in a fatal crash says new safety measures coming to that stretch of road are, in his words, a good start, though he wants more done. That comes as a 40-year-old Steinbach man died in a rollover in southeastern Manitoba over the weekend.

Two items on the watch list worth a quick mention. The Jets situation with goaltender Connor Hellebuyck remains unresolved, with no update from either side as camp approaches. And the Blue Bombers beat the Saskatchewan Roughriders in the Banjo Bowl over the long weekend, though it cost them Zach Collaros to injury.

On a lighter note, a Winnipeg sepsis survivor was reunited this week with the ICU nurse who helped keep him alive a decade ago, a reminder of the people behind the health system numbers we usually talk about.

blocks.title: Carney's Summit, an EU Reach, Alberta's Upset
blocks.script:
The story dominating Ottawa and Bay Street this week is Mark Carney's investment summit, now on its second day in Toronto. More than a hundred global investors, collectively managing over a hundred trillion dollars, are in the room, and the goal Carney has set is one trillion dollars in new investment in Canada over five years. CBC reports Canadian business leaders are pitching the country as a safe, capital-ready place to build, and are cautiously optimistic the message is landing.

Premiers came with their own lists. Manitoba's Wab Kinew is among those carrying provincial projects directly to investors, while Quebec's finance minister, Eric Girard, said he supports the calls for more private-sector investment, but he will not be endorsing specific projects, adding he was filling more of a quiet, efficient role than Manitoba's premier, given Quebec's own election campaign. Ontario put out its own list of priority projects, heavy on nuclear and mining. The Globe also reports Chinese state-backed investors joined the summit for the first time in years, a signal of a thaw with Beijing, though the Prime Minister's Office says Chinese money will face the same foreign investment screening as anyone else's. Former prime minister Stephen Harper addressed the gathering too, a cross-partisan touch as Carney tries to show, in his words, what the country can build.

Also tied to the summit, Bell Canada announced it's expanding its AI data centre near Regina, calling it the largest private investment in Saskatchewan's history, with eventual power needs of one point two gigawatts. Ottawa separately announced a billion dollars in new federal funding for agri-food processing projects, aimed at making more finished food products domestically. And sources tell the Globe that Ottawa is preparing to announce steps toward opening the four major airports to more private investment, including foreign capital, a long-simmering file in Ottawa.

On the European file, Carney heads to Strasbourg this week to pitch what he calls a unique alliance with the European Union, something short of membership. The European Parliament will open an office in Ottawa to deepen those ties, its president says. But European privacy groups are warning that Ottawa's lawful access bill, the legislation that would compel telecom and tech companies to hand data to police, could become an obstacle to any EU-Canada digital trade deal on privacy grounds. Conservative MPs have raised a different concern, warning against Canada becoming what they call the twenty-eighth EU state.

Alberta politics had its own jolt overnight. The Alberta NDP has flipped Calgary-Shaw, winning a riding held by the United Conservative Party since 2019. Campbell earned 7,461 of the 16,002 votes counted, about 47 per cent, 582 votes ahead of the UCP candidate Mike Derry. This is the first time the UCP has lost a by-election since the party was created in 2017, and it lands just over a month before the government's popularity just over a month before the Oct. 19 provincial referendum is tested at the ballot box.

Elsewhere, in British Columbia, Donegal Wilson became the seventh sitting legislator to join the new, still-unnamed party being formed by fellow former Conservative MLA Milobar, another sign of fracturing on the province's right. Quebec's five party leaders hold their first of two debates this week as that provincial campaign heats up.

On the numbers that matter to your clients: Statistics Canada says inflation held at three per cent in August, unchanged from July, as lower gas prices offset higher shelter and travel costs. Core measures, the ones the Bank of Canada watches most closely, are running nearer two per cent, part of why the Bank of Canada, on our watch list today, is widely expected to hold its rate again at its October 28th decision.

A few more worth flagging. A new report finds pandemic benefit clawbacks are still hitting low-income Canadians hardest, years after CERB. Separately, a report pegs the health and justice system cost of online harms to Canadians under 25 at up to 4.8 billion dollars a year, and Google says it will start using AI here to identify underage accounts. And Volodymyr Zelenskyy's comparison of Canada's position with the United States to Ukraine's with Russia continues to generate debate in Ottawa, even as most describe the parallel as imperfect.
talkingPoints: Carney's summit is about pledges and project lists, not signed cheques yet, so watch for follow-through over the next few months.
Manitoba is pitching hard at this summit; expect more provincial announcements tied to Port of Churchill-adjacent infrastructure in the weeks ahead.
The EU relationship is warming, but the lawful access bill is now a real sticking point for any digital trade deal.
Alberta's Calgary-Shaw upset is being read as an early signal ahead of the October 19th referendum, not a settled trend.
Inflation held at three per cent; the Bank of Canada looks set to hold again on October 28th, barring a surprise.

blocks.label: Climate Policy & Nonprofit Governance
blocks.title: Summit, Grid Bills, and Giving Gaps
blocks.script:
Mark Carney's investment summit in Toronto moves into day two today, and this is the one to watch on the energy file. Carney is set to deliver remarks and hold a press conference this afternoon, and yesterday's opening haul already included billion-dollar announcements and shifts in tax policy still being unpacked. Canada's National Observer reports Ottawa is pitching investors on a mix of conventional and clean energy, more than 40 oil, gas, and renewables projects, part of a push for a trillion dollars in capital over five years. Whether that pitch lands with the pension funds and asset managers in the room is still an open question.

The clean electricity angle worth flagging for clients: Bell's data centre expansion in Saskatchewan was one of the headline deals, described as the largest capital investment in that province's history, and it will push the facility's capacity to 1.2 gigawatts. National Observer's own analysis asks who actually pays for the electricity behind Canada's AI ambitions, and that bill is not settled. TC Energy, meanwhile, is publicly urging cooperation on expanding its gas network, after a leaked cabinet report showed Alberta pressuring the company to grow transmission capacity, and even weighing whether to take control of a pipeline network itself. That is a live standoff between a province and a major energy infrastructure name, worth watching if a client holds it.

Not everyone in Toronto is cheering the summit. National Observer reports Indigenous leaders, environmental groups, and union members marched together Monday evening opposing Carney's investment agenda, a reminder the social license for this spending push is not universal.

On nuclear, there's a useful piece from National Observer today: unanticipated shutdowns at nuclear plants are becoming more frequent as extreme weather tied to climate change increases. Worth remembering if a client treats nuclear or regulated utilities as the boring, stable part of a portfolio. Reliability is getting less boring.

Now to the charitable sector, and there are two governance stories today that matter if you advise anyone who sits on a board or runs a foundation. First, a new report cited by National Observer says there is a near total absence of effective recourse for nonprofits that get de-banked over alleged terrorism financing ties, even when those ties are thin or mistaken. If you have clients running charities with international programming, that is a real operational risk conversation.

Second, The Philanthropist Journal flags a Supreme Court ruling letting Democracy Watch keep pursuing its challenge to an ethics report tied to the WE Charity affair. Columnist Tim Harper calls it a win with real implications for how ethics oversight of charities and government dealings gets tested going forward.

On philanthropy trends, worth knowing before your next donor conversation. Imagine Canada's research, reported by Canadian Affairs, found claimed charitable donations hit $12.8 billion in 2023, up from $5.5 billion in 2000. But around nine per cent of donors account for 71 per cent of the donations, and more than half are over the age of 60. Bruce MacDonald, president and CEO of Imagine Canada, calls that pattern a straight line decline in giving among younger Canadians. For clients weighing legacy gifts or a donor advised fund, that concentration is exactly why timing and structure matter now, while that donor generation is still making decisions.

Closer to home, Efficiency Manitoba's rebate programs for heat pumps, insulation, and windows remain the main lever for building retrofits in this province, still funded through Manitoba Hydro and Centra Gas billing. Nothing new announced today, but if a client is planning a retrofit before winter, that Crown corporation is still the first call to make.
talkingPoints: Ask clients with charity boards whether their banking relationship has ever flagged international transfers.
The WE Charity ethics case is back in court, and it could reshape charity governance scrutiny.

Bell's Saskatchewan data centre deal raises a real question: who pays for the power behind Canada's AI push.

blocks.label: AI & Technology
blocks.title: Huang Calls Trump, Amodei Calls for a Pause
blocks.script:
Jensen Huang took a live phone call from Donald Trump on stage Monday at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, and put the president on speakerphone for the whole room. "The robots are not going to be taking over the world. That's not going to happen," Trump said, dismissing AI safety concerns as a hoax. Huang, dressed in his signature alligator leather jacket, was handed a foldable phone to answer it, and once he got Trump on speaker, the two seemed to agree that mounting fears about AI equate to what Trump called a hoax. TechCrunch points out Nvidia's business model depends on labs buying more chips, so downplaying existential risk is the only move if Huang cares about the share price, which is still up 33 percent for the year but fell a few points that day.

The backdrop matters. Anthropic's Dario Amodei published a 3,800 word essay over the weekend called "We Must Pace the Frontier," arguing development of the most advanced systems needs to slow down before it slips beyond human control, according to Stratechery's Ben Thompson, who notes the piece was endorsed by both Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Huang's answer, per TechCrunch's headline, was blunt: "we're not going to let that happen." Cohere's Aidan Gomez offered a different Canadian data point this week, telling the Canadian Global Growth Forum that Canada could become what BetaKit calls a data centre superpower.

Microsoft, meanwhile, drafted its own answer. TechCrunch reports the company's new AI code of conduct tells its models not to hack systems or trick humans, and lays out principles like supporting humans rather than replacing them. And MIT Technology Review flags a Google DeepMind experiment where AI agents split into factions solving math problems, and some agents actually tried to stop others from cheating, a first for this kind of whistleblowing behaviour among autonomous systems.

On the product side, OpenAI keeps buying. It picked up smartphone camera maker Glass Imaging for a reported 300 million dollars, founded by former Apple engineers who built Portrait Mode. Per Stratechery, citing CNBC, OpenAI's ad business inside ChatGPT hit a billion dollars in annualized revenue, and Amazon is now running ads inside ChatGPT too, a sign the retailer sees the chatbot as a real marketing channel even as it blocks the same bots from crawling its store. Apple's iOS 27 finally makes Siri usable day to day, and a fashion app called Daydream is using Apple Intelligence to turn your camera roll into a shopping list. And in the productivity software you actually use, Superhuman just acquired the notetaker Fathom, another sign the agentic tools market is consolidating fast.

Zoom out and the money question gets sharper. MIT Technology Review's look at the AI trillion dollar bet notes the entire boom rests on a handful of companies, meaning any wobble in spending by two or three names ripples through the whole market, worth remembering the next time a client asks why their tech-heavy fund swings on one earnings call.

On the Canadian side, Bell announced a 50 billion dollar buildout for what would be Canada's largest data centre, in Saskatchewan, a non-binding deal BetaKit says would be the largest private investment in that province's history. Intrepid Growth Partners closed its first AI fund at 525 million US, built by former OMERS and CPPIB people hunting the next generation of AI founders. LegalTech platform Closer expanded to Alberta after a three month early access run, and Define Capital picked up Synergy Gateway Verified to push into the postsecondary market, its fourth acquisition as it nears 20 million in annual recurring revenue. And at the Canada FinTech Forum, Wealthsimple's government relations lead said bluntly that the country should have had real-time payment rails five years ago, a reminder that the infrastructure your clients' money moves through is still catching up.
talkingPoints: Trump publicly waved off AI safety warnings on a live call with Nvidia's Huang, right after Anthropic's CEO called for slowing development down.
Microsoft published a written code of conduct for its AI models, a sign labs are moving from promises to documented rules.
OpenAI's ad business passed a billion dollars a year, with Amazon now buying space inside ChatGPT itself.
Bell's proposed 50 billion dollar Saskatchewan data centre would be Canada's largest, another marker of how much capital is chasing this build-out.
The AI boom's spending is concentrated in a handful of companies, so a stumble at any one of them moves the whole sector.

blocks.label: Health & Fitness
blocks.title: Spider Season Myths and Safety Tips
blocks.script: Spider season is here, and Outside has useful context if you hike or trail run this month. The number of spiders around you hasn't jumped, researchers say there aren't actually more spiders during spider season: arachnid populations stay fairly steady year-round, with hatchlings of some species overwintering in their egg sacs. What changes is behavior: this time of year the males start wandering and looking for females, so you're just bound to run into males that are out looking for a good time. The practical point: don't panic over a black widow on a fence post, brush webs off instead of swatting, and if a bite brings real pain or spreading swelling, get it checked rather than wait it out.
talkingPoints: Spider sightings spike now because males roam to mate, not because populations grow.
Treat any spreading, painful bite as a medical check, not a wait and see.

blocks.label: Parenting
blocks.title: Sport Specialization, Focus, and RESP Grants Today
blocks.script:
Start with the one a lot of hockey and ringette parents in this city are quietly worried about. The Globe and Mail looks at whether kids should specialize in one sport early, and the research consensus, including work summarized by paediatric sports medicine groups, points the other way. Athletes who specialize in a single sport before age twelve show sharply higher injury rates than those who play multiple sports, with some studies putting the increase at seventy percent or more, driven by overuse injuries in the same muscles and joints. The Canadian Paediatric Society's broader position has been that unstructured, varied play builds more resilient athletes and reduces burnout. If a client's kid is being pushed toward one sport, year round, before puberty, that is worth a gentle question, not a celebration.

Next, a Globe advice column addresses a question a lot of parents ask privately: what to do when a child stops taking their own schoolwork seriously. The core guidance there is to shift consequences and ownership back onto the child rather than the parent absorbing the stress, so the child experiences the natural results of missed work.

On breakfast, the Globe and Mail rounds up evidence that a nutritious morning meal helps kids concentrate and learn better at school, with protein and complex carbohydrates doing more for sustained focus than sugary cereal.

There is also a ScienceDaily item on brain wiring that is really an adult cognition story, not a childhood one, but it is worth a sentence for clients thinking about aging parents alongside young kids. Researchers found that short range wiring just beneath the brain's surface may help protect language skills even as gray matter shrinks with age, a reminder that cognitive decline is not a single, simple curve.

On the money side, the federal Canada Education Savings Grant remains the workhorse for RESP planning. Government of Canada figures confirm the grant matches twenty percent of the first two thousand five hundred dollars contributed each year, up to five hundred dollars annually, with a seven thousand two hundred dollar lifetime cap per child. Lower income families can also access the Canada Learning Bond, up to two thousand dollars per child, with no contribution required. For clients with a baby this year, opening that account early still matters more than the amount inside it.
talkingPoints: Early single sport specialization raises injury risk before age twelve, per paediatric sports medicine research.
Shift schoolwork ownership to the child, not the parent, when motivation slips.
A protein forward breakfast supports school focus better than sugary options.
Brain wiring research suggests cognitive decline is not one straight line.
RESP grant matching tops out at seven thousand two hundred dollars per child, open the account early.

blocks.label: Sports
blocks.title: Kawhi Returns to Toronto as NFL Week One Dazzles
blocks.script:
Good morning. It has been a busy weekend across the sports world, from the NBA to the gridiron to Flushing Meadows. Here is your roundup.

We start with the Los Angeles Clippers. Owner Steve Ballmer announced Sunday night that his franchise will accept the severe penalties handed down by the NBA for circumventing the league's salary cap rules to funnel money to Kawhi Leonard. Ballmer said he had, in his words, sincere regrets about the situation. According to the Globe and Mail, the Clippers have now paid a thirty million dollar fine. With that settled, the Raptors and Clippers have completed the trade sending Leonard back to Toronto, the city where he led the franchise to its 2019 championship.

Turning to the NFL, Week One delivered a scoring frenzy, according to The Athletic. The New York Giants beat the visiting Dallas Cowboys 28-20 in a game that felt more lopsided than the score suggested. In Minnesota, backup quarterback Carson Wentz threw three touchdown passes, two to Justin Jefferson, as the Vikings stormed back to beat Green Bay 39-22 after starter Kyler Murray left with a concussion.

It was a rough day for the Los Angeles Rams. Head coach Sean McVay said the season opener made clear that star pass rusher Myles Garrett needs knee surgery, according to the Globe and Mail. Garrett had no tackles or sacks in the loss to San Francisco and is expected to miss at least four games.

In Chicago, quarterback Caleb Williams and coach Ben Johnson had the Bears rolling, scoring 59 points behind two passing and two rushing touchdowns. The Cincinnati Bengals beat Tampa Bay 33-27 with a pick six off Joe Burrow, while the Baltimore Ravens exploded for 41 points under their new coaching staff. Buffalo's Josh Allen also had a big day, throwing and running for two touchdowns apiece in a win, the Globe and Mail reports.

It was a different story in Cleveland. The Browns were routed 34-10 by Jacksonville, and Deshaun Watson struggled again, prompting fresh questions from The Athletic about how much longer the franchise can keep investing in him. And in New Orleans, the Saints lost a heartbreaker in overtime to Detroit, 31-30, on a disputed replay call.

Over in tennis, Alexander Zverev is the U.S. Open men's singles champion after beating American Ben Shelton in four sets, The Athletic reports. It is Zverev's second Grand Slam title and cements his place among the game's elite this season. In other tennis news, Canada's Gabriel Diallo has withdrawn from the Davis Cup tie against France because of a leg injury, according to CBC Sports.

In baseball, the playoff picture is starting to take shape. The Tampa Bay Rays clinched a spot with a walk-off home run from Junior Caminero, and the Milwaukee Brewers clinched minutes later with a 20-0 blowout of Cincinnati, The Athletic reports. The National League race is tightening behind Atlanta and the Dodgers, while the Cubs, Phillies and Padres are jammed together in the wild card hunt.

In hockey, the Montreal Canadiens have signed head coach Martin St. Louis to a multi-year extension after he guided the team to consecutive playoff berths, according to CBC Sports and the Globe and Mail. In Colorado, Joe Sakic plans to stay on indefinitely as Avalanche general manager with no search underway, the Globe and Mail reports.

Elsewhere, UFC heavyweight champion Tom Aspinall has vacated his title due to ongoing complications from an eye injury, The Athletic reports. Calgary will host the Winter X Games in February, CBC Sports says. And at the wheelchair basketball world championships in Ottawa, host Canada's men were eliminated by Poland in the round of sixteen, while the Canadian women remain undefeated.

blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Reading the yield curve: shape, inversion, and what it has and has not predicted / RESP: grants, the CESG, and withdrawal strategy for EAPs versus contributions / Numbers people can hear: translating figures into comparisons and consequences
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Macro & rates, lesson 2: Reading the yield curve: shape, inversion, and what it has and has not predicted.

The yield curve is just government bond yields lined up by maturity, three month, two year, ten year, thirty year, for the same issuer. Normally it slopes upward, because lending money for thirty years carries more risk than lending it for three months, so investors demand more yield for the wait. When that flips, when short-term yields sit above long-term yields, that is inversion, and it means the market expects the central bank to cut rates later because it thinks growth or inflation is weakening.

Here is the real example. In July 2023, the US two-year Treasury yield hit roughly four point eight six percent while the ten-year sat near three point seven eight percent. That is a spread of about negative one point zero eight, the deepest two-year, ten-year inversion since 1981, reported widely at the time including by the Wall Street Journal. That curve stayed inverted for about two years before steepening again through 2024 and into 2025.

Now the mistake. People treat inversion as a countdown clock, as if recession follows in six months on schedule. It does not work that way. The lag between inversion and any downturn has ranged from six months to over two years historically, and there have been inversions, like in 1998, that produced no recession at all. What actually matters more is the re-steepening after inversion, when the curve moves back to normal shape, because that has historically lined up closer to the start of downturns than the inversion itself. The curve tells you what bond investors expect for rates and growth. It does not tell you timing, and it says nothing about which sectors or companies get hit hardest, that is a separate layer of work.

For today, pull up the Canada and US government yield curves on Thomson ONE, the GOVT screen works, and note the two year, five year, ten year, and thirty year yields for both. Check whether either curve is inverted right now, and compare today's spread to where it sat six months ago.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 6: RESP: grants, the CESG, and withdrawal strategy for EAPs versus contributions.

The Registered Education Savings Plan, or RESP, is the only account where the government hands you free money just for contributing. That's the Canada Education Savings Grant, the CESG. For 2026, the rule is 20 percent on the first 2,500 dollars you contribute per beneficiary per year, so a maximum grant of 500 dollars a year. Lifetime CESG per child caps at 7,200 dollars. Lifetime contribution room per child is 50,000 dollars, no annual cap on contributions, just no extra grant past that 2,500 dollar sweet spot. Manitoba has no provincial top-up here, unlike Quebec's QESI. What you get in Manitoba is the federal CESG plus, for lower income families, the Canada Learning Bond, up to 2,000 dollars, paid with no contribution required at all.

Here's the withdrawal side, and this is where advisors earn their fee. Money coming out for school splits into two buckets. Post-Secondary Education withdrawals, PSE, are just your original contributions back, no tax, ever. Educational Assistance Payments, EAP, are the grant money plus all the growth, and that's taxed in the student's hands. Budget 2023 raised the EAP cap for the first 13 weeks of enrollment to 8,000 dollars for full-time students, up from 5,000. After those 13 weeks, no cap.

Worked example. A student starts university in September 2026. The RESP holds 40,000 dollars: 28,000 in contributions, 12,000 in grant and growth. Withdraw 8,000 dollars as EAP in year one. The student has little or no other income, so that 8,000 lands mostly or entirely under the basic personal amount and gets taxed at close to zero.

The mistake: families draw PSE first because it feels safer, "it's just my own money." That leaves the taxable EAP piling up for later years, when the student might be working part-time and actually paying tax on it, or worse, the program ends early and unused grant money has to be repaid to the government.

Your task today, ten minutes: pull one client's RESP statement, split the balance into contribution room used versus grant and growth, and write down which bucket you'd draw from first if withdrawals started this year.

Communication, lesson 5: Numbers people can hear: translating figures into comparisons and consequences.

You're in a board meeting. The finance chair says, "revenue grew 40 percent this year." Everyone nods. Nobody feels anything, because 40 percent of what.

That's the whole lesson: a number without a comparison is just a sound. A number with a comparison becomes a fact people can carry out of the room.

Chip Heath, the Stanford professor who wrote "Made to Stick" with his brother Dan, studied why some numbers stick and others vanish. The answer isn't precision, it's scale the listener already understands.

Worked example. A food bank tells its board, "we distributed 1.4 million pounds of food last year." True, but it slides past you. Reframe it: 1.4 million pounds is roughly 1,150,000 meals, or about 3,150 meals every single day the doors were open, or one meal every 27 seconds. Now the board member pictures a person eating, not a spreadsheet cell.

Same move works with money. The Chronicle of Philanthropy reported total US charitable giving hit 557 billion dollars in 2023. Say instead: that's roughly 1,700 dollars given, on average, for every person in the country, whether they gave a cent or not. That comparison makes a huge, abstract number personal.

The mistake almost everyone makes: leading with the percentage and skipping the base number. "We grew 40 percent" tells you nothing about size. Going from 10 clients to 14 is 40 percent. Going from 10,000 to 14,000 is also 40 percent. Always give the base, then the change, then what it means for the person in front of you.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: On Thomson ONE, pull the Canada and US two year and ten year government yields, calculate the spread for each, and write down whether it is inverted and how that compares to six months ago.
Financial Planning Facts: Pull one RESP statement, separate the balance into contributions versus grant and growth, and note which bucket to draw first if withdrawals started this year.

Communication: Pull one statistic you use often, a client win, a board metric, a LinkedIn claim. Rewrite it three ways: as a rate per day or per person, as a comparison to something the listener already knows the size of, and as a consequence for one real person.

Now the mistake. People treat inversion as a countdown clock, as if recession follows in six months on schedule. It does not work that way. The lag between inversion and any downturn has ranged from six months to over two years historically, and there have been inversions, like in 1998, that produced no recession at all. What actually matters more is the re-steepening after inversion, when the curve moves back to normal shape, because that has historically lined up closer to the start of downturns than the inversion itself. The curve tells you what bond investors expect for rates and growth. It does not tell you timing, and it says nothing about which sectors or companies get hit hardest, that is a separate layer of work.

For today, pull up the Canada and US government yield curves on Thomson ONE, the GOVT screen works, and note the two year, five year, ten year, and thirty year yields for both. Check whether either curve is inverted right now, and compare today's spread to where it sat six months ago.
lessons.task: On Thomson ONE, pull the Canada and US two year and ten year government yields, calculate the spread for each, and write down whether it is inverted and how that compares to six months ago.

lessons.label: Financial Planning Facts
lessons.title: RESP: grants, the CESG, and withdrawal strategy for EAPs versus contributions
lessons.script:
The Registered Education Savings Plan, or RESP, is the only account where the government hands you free money just for contributing. That's the Canada Education Savings Grant, the CESG. For 2026, the rule is 20 percent on the first 2,500 dollars you contribute per beneficiary per year, so a maximum grant of 500 dollars a year. Lifetime CESG per child caps at 7,200 dollars. Lifetime contribution room per child is 50,000 dollars, no annual cap on contributions, just no extra grant past that 2,500 dollar sweet spot. Manitoba has no provincial top-up here, unlike Quebec's QESI. What you get in Manitoba is the federal CESG plus, for lower income families, the Canada Learning Bond, up to 2,000 dollars, paid with no contribution required at all.

Here's the withdrawal side, and this is where advisors earn their fee. Money coming out for school splits into two buckets. Post-Secondary Education withdrawals, PSE, are just your original contributions back, no tax, ever. Educational Assistance Payments, EAP, are the grant money plus all the growth, and that's taxed in the student's hands. Budget 2023 raised the EAP cap for the first 13 weeks of enrollment to 8,000 dollars for full-time students, up from 5,000. After those 13 weeks, no cap.

Worked example. A student starts university in September 2026. The RESP holds 40,000 dollars: 28,000 in contributions, 12,000 in grant and growth. Withdraw 8,000 dollars as EAP in year one. The student has little or no other income, so that 8,000 lands mostly or entirely under the basic personal amount and gets taxed at close to zero.

The mistake: families draw PSE first because it feels safer, "it's just my own money." That leaves the taxable EAP piling up for later years, when the student might be working part-time and actually paying tax on it, or worse, the program ends early and unused grant money has to be repaid to the government.

Your task today, ten minutes: pull one client's RESP statement, split the balance into contribution room used versus grant and growth, and write down which bucket you'd draw from first if withdrawals started this year.
lessons.task: Pull one RESP statement, separate the balance into contributions versus grant and growth, and note which bucket to draw first if withdrawals started this year.

lessons.label: Communication
lessons.title: Numbers people can hear: translating figures into comparisons and consequences
lessons.script:
You're in a board meeting. The finance chair says, "revenue grew 40 percent this year." Everyone nods. Nobody feels anything, because 40 percent of what.

That's the whole lesson: a number without a comparison is just a sound. A number with a comparison becomes a fact people can carry out of the room.

Chip Heath, the Stanford professor who wrote "Made to Stick" with his brother Dan, studied why some numbers stick and others vanish. The answer isn't precision, it's scale the listener already understands.

Worked example. A food bank tells its board, "we distributed 1.4 million pounds of food last year." True, but it slides past you. Reframe it: 1.4 million pounds is roughly 1,150,000 meals, or about 3,150 meals every single day the doors were open, or one meal every 27 seconds. Now the board member pictures a person eating, not a spreadsheet cell.

Same move works with money. The Chronicle of Philanthropy reported total US charitable giving hit 557 billion dollars in 2023. Say instead: that's roughly 1,700 dollars given, on average, for every person in the country, whether they gave a cent or not. That comparison makes a huge, abstract number personal.

The mistake almost everyone makes: leading with the percentage and skipping the base number. "We grew 40 percent" tells you nothing about size. Going from 10 clients to 14 is 40 percent. Going from 10,000 to 14,000 is also 40 percent. Always give the base, then the change, then what it means for the person in front of you.
lessons.task: Pull one statistic you use often, a client win, a board metric, a LinkedIn claim. Rewrite it three ways: as a rate per day or per person, as a comparison to something the listener already knows the size of, and as a consequence for one real person.
lessons.drill: Record yourself saying the original stat cold, ten seconds. Then record your rewritten version. Play both, unlabeled, to one other person. Ask them to repeat back what they remember thirty seconds later. Pass: they repeat the translated version accurately. Fail: they repeat the raw number, the wrong number, or nothing at all.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Oil Shock, Rate Bets, and Carney's Investment Push
blocks.script:
Start with oil, because it touches almost everything else you'll talk about with clients this week. Saudi Arabia has shut down its East-West pipeline after drone attacks over the weekend, and that route carries about seven million barrels a day across the kingdom to Red Sea ports, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz entirely. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said it suspended operations on the pipeline as a precaution after multiple attacks, and the pipeline is critical in linking oil production sites in the Eastern Province with Yanbu on the kingdom's western coast, with full pumping capacity of about seven million barrels per day. Brent crude touched 108 US dollars a barrel this morning before easing back, and West Texas Intermediate is trading around 103. Brent crude rose as high as 108, while U.S. crude oil touched 103 per barrel. Layer on top of that a postponed diplomatic meeting between Iran and Gulf states over the Strait of Hormuz, and reports that Saudi export stocks at one port could run dry within five to seven days, and you've got a genuine supply scare, not just headline noise. Tell clients this matters for two reasons: pump prices, and inflation readings that feed straight into central bank decisions.

Which brings you to today's number. Statistics Canada releases the August Consumer Price Index this morning, and the Street is watching closely. A poll of economists expects the annual rate of inflation was three per cent last month, holding steady from July. Economists expect the headline CPI to remain unchanged at 3 per cent year over year, with the Bank of Canada's core measure forecast to rise by just 0.1 per cent. The story underneath the headline is energy. RBC economists say Canada has seen inflationary pressure coming mainly from higher energy prices, which are up around 23 per cent from a year ago, though there was slight relief at the pumps last month compared with earlier this summer. Grocery inflation has also been running hotter than the headline number for about a year and a half, so lower income households are still feeling squeezed even as the topline print looks tame.

On the Bank of Canada, and this one's on your watch list, the bank held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent at its September 2nd meeting. The August inflation figures come after the Bank of Canada left its key policy rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent earlier this month, and the central bank has held its policy rate steady in seven consecutive decisions as it tries to balance volatile global energy prices and U.S. tariffs hampering the economy. The next scheduled decision is October 28th, and most economists still expect another hold, but Governor Tiff Macklem has flagged that if rising energy costs start spilling into the price of other goods and services, a hike becomes live. Wednesday brings the bank's summary of deliberations, which should give you a clearer read on how seriously they're weighing the trade war and the Middle East conflict together. If a client asks you point blank whether the BoC is done cutting, the honest answer is that the bar for a move either way just got higher, and the risk has tilted toward a hike in early 2027 rather than a cut.

South of the border, this is shaping up as a pivotal week for central banks generally. The Federal Reserve decides Wednesday, followed by the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan on successive days. Markets have swung toward pricing in a Fed hike, not a cut, after a hotter than expected core inflation print Friday. JPMorgan's chief US economist put it plainly, that the Fed risks its credibility if it doesn't back up its rhetoric with action. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is now navigating this in direct tension with President Trump, who's been pushing publicly for lower rates. That's an unusual dynamic to explain to clients: a central bank that may hike specifically because inflation is proving stickier than politically convenient.

Equity markets are reacting to two things at once, the oil shock and a sudden wave of caution out of the artificial intelligence industry. Anthropic's CEO published an open letter over the weekend calling for a slowdown in AI development and pledged to do so unilaterally, and OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and others echoed the call. That's rattled the exact stocks that have carried this market's momentum. SoftBank shares dropped double digits in Tokyo, memory chip makers in Korea and Japan fell hard, and Nvidia was down in US premarket trading this morning. Nasdaq futures are leading losses. Here in Canada, TSX futures are following that lower ahead of the inflation print, even though Friday's session was actually positive, up about half a percent, led by names like Boyd Group and Celestica. Tell clients this is a valuation and momentum story on top of a supply shock story, and that the two are reinforcing each other right now rather than offsetting.

On currency, the loonie is weaker again today. The Canadian dollar weakened against its U.S. counterpart, trading in a range of 71.92 to 72.13 US cents, down about 0.17 per cent over the past month. A stronger US dollar index and rising rate expectations south of the border are the main drag. For anyone with US dollar exposure or upcoming cross-border spending, this is worth a quick mention.

Now the domestic story that's actually dominating Bay Street this week, even more than rates: the Canada Investment Summit running today and tomorrow in Toronto. Prime Minister Carney is pitching the country to roughly two dozen sources' worth of global capital, with a goal of one trillion dollars in investment over five years. More than 160 projects are on the table, including a proposed high speed rail link between Edmonton and Calgary and a Port of Churchill expansion, which matters to anyone in this room with Manitoba exposure, and Manitoba Hydro is worth watching if energy infrastructure spending flows this way. TD committed 150 billion dollars and Scotiabank committed 100 billion dollars this morning to fund Canadian companies in critical sectors, and Scotiabank has also brought on former US ambassador Kirsten Hillman to advise its new Scotia Growth Institute, which is on your watch list too. On trade, Trump told reporters this weekend a Canada-US deal could come fairly soon, and Carney has echoed that he doesn't expect further retaliation from either side. That's a meaningfully more constructive tone than we've had in months.

One more thread worth a sentence with clients: Canada is quietly exploring deeper ties with the European Union, possibly even some kind of associate status, as a hedge against overreliance on Washington. And on housing, the Globe's own reporting this morning flags that the market should brace for more strain heading into 2027, tied to affordability and borrowing costs that aren't falling as fast as some homeowners had hoped. Worth keeping on your radar for renewal conversations this fall.
talkingPoints: Oil just spiked on a Saudi pipeline shutdown, and that's the wildcard for both inflation and your energy holdings this week.
Today's Canadian inflation number is expected to hold near 3 per cent, with the Bank of Canada watching whether energy costs bleed into everything else.
The Bank of Canada's rate decision is on the watch list, next one October 28th, and a hike in early 2027 is now a real possibility, not a hold forever story.
The Fed decides Wednesday and markets are now betting on a hike, not a cut, which is an awkward message for anyone expecting lower borrowing costs soon.
Carney's trillion dollar investment summit in Toronto, plus TD and Scotiabank's big financing commitments, is the most constructive Canadian growth story we've had in a while.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: AI Giants Call for Slowdown as Markets Wobble
blocks.script:
Good evening. Here is your roundup of the day's top business and world news.

The biggest story tonight comes from Silicon Valley, where the leaders of the world's largest AI companies are suddenly talking about hitting the brakes. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an open letter over the weekend calling for a global slowdown in AI development, according to Bloomberg's Markets Daily newsletter. Amodei warned that AI has been advancing drastically faster this summer, driven by the technology's growing ability to build its own successors, and said this risks AI outrunning humanity's ability to understand and control it.

Amodei also committed Anthropic to giving outside evaluators permanent, employee-level access to its systems so they can check safety measures and flag problems.

He wasn't alone. OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk all backed the call for a slower pace, Bloomberg reports. Altman said OpenAI would offer similar access to independent evaluators, and confirmed he's pushing the company's planned stock market listing back to at least 2027, calling this an ill-advised moment to go public.

Not everyone is convinced this is really about safety. White House AI chief David Sacks described the industry's sudden caution as a bid for regulatory capture, according to The Peak newsletter. President Trump himself has downplayed the warnings, according to the BBC, suggesting that concerns are being raised by, in his words, negative forces worried about things that won't happen, and pointing to competition with China as a reason to keep pushing forward.

Meanwhile, a former Anthropic researcher told the BBC that AI safety staff are genuinely frightened for humanity's future, even as the BBC also reports that some in Silicon Valley are treating the dramatic warnings with skepticism. In Britain, MPs and members of the House of Lords are calling for new legislation to address AI's threat to human rights, arguing existing law isn't equipped to handle it. And former President Obama has urged Democrats to develop a clear plan on AI safeguards, calling it a central issue the party needs to address.

Markets felt the jitters immediately. Bloomberg's Markets Daily reports that AI bellwether stocks took a hit, with SoftBank shares sliding eleven percent in Tokyo. Chipmakers were hammered too, with South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung both down sharply, and Europe's ASML falling more than four percent. In the United States, Nvidia and memory chip makers were lower in premarket trading. On the flip side, software companies seen as less exposed to an AI slowdown, including Adobe, Salesforce, and Crowdstrike, all gained ground.

Adding to market anxiety, oil prices jumped after Saudi Arabia was forced to close a major crude pipeline following drone attacks, according to Bloomberg. Traders say as much as four percent of global oil supply could be at risk, on top of ongoing disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, where a planned meeting between Iran and Gulf nations on the shipping lane has reportedly been postponed. Separately, Yemen's Houthi rebels have seized more islands in the southern Red Sea, according to the Globe and Mail, tightening their grip on a major maritime route and prompting Somali shippers to look for alternative paths.

Turning to Canada, Prime Minister Mark Carney is kicking off his Canada Investment Summit in Toronto this week, seeking roughly one trillion dollars in commitments from major global investors, according to CBC. More than 167 projects are reportedly on the table. Canadian banks are already lining up behind the effort. The Globe and Mail reports TD has committed 150 billion dollars to fund Canadian companies in critical sectors over five years, while Scotiabank has pledged more than 100 billion dollars for similar expansion, tapping former U.S. ambassador Kirsten Hillman to help lead the push. Protests are also planned around the summit, with organizers objecting to putting the country's economic future in the hands of corporate executives, the Globe and Mail reports.

On trade, President Trump told reporters over the weekend that a deal between the U.S. and Canada could be coming fairly soon, downplaying talk of the U.S. walking away from the CUSMA agreement, according to The Peak. Carney struck a similarly optimistic note last week, saying he doesn't expect further tariff retaliation from either side. Separately, CBC reports Canadian exports to China rose about 30 percent in the first half of 2026, even as imports from China declined, according to data from the Canada-China Business Council and the University of Alberta.

In Europe, exit polls show Sweden's centre-left bloc winning the country's parliamentary election, a result that bucks the rightward trend seen elsewhere on the continent, Reuters reports via The Peak. The result was described as an unexpectedly poor showing for the right-wing Sweden Democrats.

And in Britain, Prime Minister Burnham is urging a culture shift in how the UK does business, saying risk-takers deserve government backing, even as his administration faces criticism for raising business costs, the BBC reports. Separately, property website Zoopla forecasts rents in the UK will accelerate, rising four to five percent a year by December.
talkingPoints: Major AI firms including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind are calling for a slower pace of development, citing loss-of-control risks, while critics call it regulatory capture.
Global markets wobbled on the AI slowdown talk and on oil price spikes following attacks on Saudi pipeline infrastructure and ongoing Red Sea and Hormuz disruptions.
Canada's Carney is seeking roughly a trillion dollars in investment commitments at a Toronto summit this week, backed by major bank pledges, amid protests and trade talks with Washington.

blocks.label: Practice: Tax, Regulatory & Industry
blocks.title: Registered Plans, CIRO Breach, and Rate Watch
blocks.script:
Start with the one that affects how you talk to every client this week. The Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, that's CIRO, the national self-regulator for investment and mutual fund dealers, is still working through its cybersecurity incident. CIRO has confirmed the breach hit registration data, not the National Registration Database itself, and the organization began sending letters to affected individuals beginning September 9. That's this week. If you get calls from clients who received one of those letters, the message is simple: their trading system wasn't touched, this is registration information CIRO holds, and CIRO has said it's conducting a renewed review of its data retention policies. Worth raising proactively with anyone who's had a CIRO-registered advisor over the years, even ones they've since left.

Layer onto that a second CIRO story that's more about your own file hygiene. New proficiency rules took effect January 1 this year, meaning newly approved registered representatives need a relevant diploma or degree, or four years of relevant experience, before they get approved. And on the documentation side, CIRO hearing panels have been sanctioning firms over what is or isn't in the client file. National Bank Financial accepted a settlement this past March over a failure to properly supervise note-taking and suitability documentation on one representative's book. CIRO's also running a Rule Consolidation Project that will reshape know-your-client and suitability documentation once finalized. Translation for your practice: your meeting notes need to show the reasoning, not just the recommendation.

Now the numbers you'll actually use in review meetings this fall. The 2026 Registered Retirement Savings Plan dollar limit is $33,810, up from $32,490 in 2025. Remember that's capped at 18 percent of prior year earned income, so a client earning $150,000 gets roughly $27,000 in new room, not the full dollar limit. Tax-Free Savings Account room added another $7,000 on January 1, same as the past two years, which puts cumulative room at $109,000 for anyone eligible since 2009 who's never contributed. First Home Savings Account holders get $8,000 of new room a year toward a $40,000 lifetime cap, and withdrawals for a qualifying first home stay tax-free. Registered Education Savings Plan lifetime contribution room per beneficiary is $50,000. For your incorporated business owners and physicians, this is the moment to revisit the salary versus dividend decision before year-end bonus declarations, since RRSP room only builds off salaried, T4 income, not dividends.

On the macro side, Statistics Canada put out August inflation this morning, and the Street was looking for headline Consumer Price Index growth to hold around 3 percent, unchanged from July, per Investment Executive and the Globe and Mail. Gasoline was still running about 23 percent above year-ago levels even after easing in August, RBC economist Nathan Janzen noted. Core measures, which strip out food and energy, are sitting closer to 2 percent, and that's what the Bank of Canada actually watches. The Globe reports another hold looks likely at the Bank's October 28 decision, though Governor Tiff Macklem has flagged he'd consider hiking if energy costs spill into broader prices. That decision stays on your watch list heading into the fourth quarter.

On the industry side, both TD and Scotiabank made headlines today with big Canadian financing commitments tied to the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto. TD is putting $150 billion toward Canadian companies in critical sectors over five years, and Scotiabank, parent of Scotia Wealth Management, is committing $100 billion. That's on your watch list given the Scotia Wealth Management connection, and it signals both banks leaning harder into domestic corporate lending as Ottawa tries to court foreign capital. Separately, CIBC earmarked $2 billion for small and medium-sized defence firms, part of the same push to scale domestic manufacturing capacity.

On product and fee trends, Advisor.ca flags rising client interest in annuities, driven by higher interest rates making guaranteed income products more attractive again. Worth raising with any client approaching retirement or already in a life transition, since a rate environment like this one is exactly when annuities start pricing more competitively against a pure drawdown strategy. Investment Executive's product roundup also shows Vanguard launching an actively managed fixed-income exchange-traded fund, alongside new offerings from Manulife, Capstone, Hamilton ETFs, Corton Capital and Smead Canada. Active strategies keep pushing into ETF wrappers, and that's worth a line in any fee conversation this month.

Two more for your file. A former tech executive resolved a Securities and Exchange Commission insider trading case in the U.S. after trading ahead of negative earnings news, a reminder to keep pre-clearance conversations current with any client who sits on a board or has material non-public information exposure. And closer to home, the Globe reports a second TD investor has alleged fraudulent trades in an obscure Chinese stock, following an earlier Alberta case with what sounds like an identical pattern. Given the CIRO breach news, this is a good week to walk clients through how to spot unauthorized account activity.

Last one, and it touches your professional client base directly. The Globe reports on Canadian students going abroad for medical school because of competitive domestic admissions, often at substantially higher cost. If you advise young physicians, that debt load now shows up years before incorporation and passive income planning even start, so factor it into any new physician's five-year plan before you talk about setting up a professional corporation.
talkingPoints: The CIRO breach letters going out this week are about registration data, not trading access, so reassure before you explain.
New RRSP room for 2026 is $33,810, but it's still capped at 18 percent of earned income, so check the math before promising a number.
TFSA cumulative room is now $109,000 for anyone who's never contributed since 2009.
Rising rates are pulling annuities back into retirement income conversations, worth a mention with anyone near retirement.
