blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Hydro Tariffs, Bank of Canada Hold, Daycare Scandal
blocks.script:
The story with the biggest dollar signs for your clients today is Manitoba Hydro, and it is two stories rolled into one. The Canada-U.S. trade war has complicated Manitoba Hydro's plan to buy gas turbines for its $3-billion Brandon generating station expansion from a manufacturer based in Massachusetts. Layer onto that the fact that six weeks of public hearings into Manitoba Hydro's generating plans came to an end with more criticism of the Crown corporation's proposed natural gas expansion in Brandon. If you have clients with Hydro bonds, Hydro pension exposure, or just a mortgage tied to provincial rate assumptions, this is worth watching. A three billion dollar capital project running into tariff friction on its main equipment supplier is the kind of thing that shows up later as a rate application.

Speaking of rates, the Bank of Canada is on your watch list, and it held its target for the overnight rate at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%, on September second. That makes a seventh consecutive hold. The Bank flagged the war in the Middle East and new US tariffs as live risks to inflation, language it used to justify staying put rather than cutting further. The next scheduled date for announcing the overnight rate target is October 28, 2026. So if a client asks why nothing moved, tell them that is your next real decision point.

Closer to home, CBC Manitoba has a story that will come up at any board table this week: a five and a half million dollar daycare, built two years ago with provincial funds in the East St. Paul area, is now sitting vacant, plundered by scavengers, and damaged by flooding. That is public money, spent on a facility meant to add child care spaces in a province that has spent years talking up its child care expansion, and it is now a boarded up shell. Expect questions about how that gets audited and who signed off on it.

On the trade file, CBC reports Manitoba sports organizations and retailers are pushing governments on both sides of the border to suspend tariffs on sports equipment, warning that higher prices could reduce participation in youth and recreational sports. For retail clients or anyone with exposure to sporting goods distribution in this province, that is a small but real margin squeeze story, and it lines up with the broader tariff drag the Bank of Canada itself is watching.

Manitoba's other big engine, agriculture, got a research update from CBC Manitoba out of Brandon, where scientists at Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada are racing to breed crops that can handle heat and drought, work aimed squarely at protecting yields on the hundreds of acres surrounding the city. If you have farm clients in the Westman region, or bank shares tied to grain handling, that research pipeline is part of what protects revenue when the growing season turns hostile.

On the Blue Bombers, also on your watch list, Winnipeg beat Saskatchewan nineteen to six at the Banjo Bowl on Saturday at Princess Auto Stadium. Safety Redha Kramdi, back from a broken hand, played what CBC called a huge role in the win. Good dinner table material this week if you have Bomber season ticket holders as clients.

Finally, three community stories worth knowing even if they are not balance sheet items. Steinbach held its Pride event this weekend after last year's was postponed over safety threats, and CBC reports marchers said they were not going to hide. About one hundred people gathered at The Forks for the third annual Fentanyl Awareness walk. And the family of Tanya Nepinak marked fifteen years since she went missing in Winnipeg's West End, a reminder that cases like hers still shape how this city talks about policing priorities.

That is Manitoba and Winnipeg for today.

blocks.label: Canadian Politics
blocks.title: Carney's Toronto Pitch, Hydro's Trade War Headache
blocks.script:
Prime Minister Mark Carney spent Sunday night in Toronto trying to turn a headline number into real deals. The Canada Investment Summit opened at the Royal Ontario Museum, and the room included premiers, cabinet ministers and executives from BlackRock, RBC, Scotiabank and CPP Investments. Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew was on the guest list alongside the other provincial leaders. Carney told the crowd that investors managing over 120 trillion dollars in assets are looking at Canada differently now, and that there's a new consensus from Iqaluit to Victoria that the country is taking control of its future. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says she expects the summit, running through Tuesday at the Four Seasons, to produce actual deal announcements, not just talk. Officials have circulated a list of more than 160 projects open for investment, and two are worth flagging for a Manitoba audience: a proposed 57 billion dollar expansion at the Port of Churchill, and a 10.9 billion dollar high speed rail link between Edmonton and Calgary. On the financing side, TD committed 150 billion dollars and Scotiabank committed 100 billion dollars to fund Canadian companies over the next five years. Scotia Wealth Management's parent bank making that kind of commitment is on the watch list worth noting for clients who ask where the big banks are putting capital.

Statistics Canada put out August inflation numbers this morning. The Street expected headline CPI to hold at 3 percent year over year, unchanged from July, with gasoline still running about 23 percent above last year despite easing slightly last month. Grocery inflation has outpaced the overall rate for roughly a year and a half, which keeps squeezing lower income households hardest. Core measures, which strip out food and energy, are running closer to 2 percent, and that's what the Bank of Canada watches most closely. The Bank of Canada rate decision is on the watch list: another hold is expected October 28, though Governor Tiff Macklem has said the bank would consider raising rates if energy costs spill into broader prices. Most economists don't see a hike this year, but the odds of one in early 2027 are rising.

Closer to home, Manitoba Hydro is on the watch list and had a rough couple of weeks. Six weeks of public hearings into the utility's generating plans wrapped up with continued criticism of its proposal to expand natural gas burning at its Brandon station. Separately, the Canada-US trade war has complicated Manitoba Hydro's plan to buy gas turbines for that same three billion dollar Brandon expansion from a Massachusetts manufacturer. That's a direct, local example of how tariff friction is showing up in provincial infrastructure planning, not just in the news out of Ottawa.

On the diplomatic front, Carney is set to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday. Ottawa wants deeper trade, investment, security and labour ties with the European Union, but a senior government official says not at the expense of Canadian sovereignty. The Wall Street Journal reported Carney had floated the idea of Canada as an associate member of the EU, though a Canadian government source pushed back, saying it was the EU, not Carney, that raised the idea, and that any formal arrangement is premature. Carney also meets his British counterpart this week for the first time, and travels to Saint-Pierre and Miquelon next week to meet French President Emmanuel Macron on energy and defence.

None of this happens separate from the tariff fight with Washington. Canada and the US remain stuck in their trade war positions, and some Democratic politicians in Washington argue a strong showing for their party in the November midterms would shift Trump's approach to Canada. That's a bet, not a certainty, and it's one more reason the investment summit's emphasis on non-US capital, from European and Gulf investors, matters for how exposed Canadian portfolios are to a single trading partner.

TD and Scotiabank each pledged nine and ten figure sums to Canadian business financing this week, a signal on where bank capital is heading.
August inflation held near 3 percent, but the Bank of Canada watches core inflation near 2 percent, with the next rate decision October 28.

blocks.label: Climate Policy & Nonprofit Governance
blocks.title: Manitoba Gas Fight, Ottawa's Investment Pitch, United Way's Record Year
blocks.script:
The biggest energy story out of Manitoba this week wrapped up last Wednesday. Six weeks of public hearings into Manitoba Hydro's generating plan closed with more pushback on the utility's proposal to burn more natural gas, CBC News reports. Six weeks of public hearings into Manitoba Hydro's generating plans came to an end with more criticism of the Crown corporation's proposed natural gas expansion in Brandon, and the Public Utilities Board spent late July to early September scrutinizing the integrated resource plan. That plan calls for 1,760 more megawatts of electricity, more than a quarter of Hydro's existing generating capacity, over the next decade. It leans on 600 megawatts of new Indigenous majority owned wind power, but also roughly 750 megawatts of new gas turbines, and several groups told the board in closing arguments that Hydro hadn't made its case for the gas piece.

That matters for anyone with Manitoba Hydro exposure or rate sensitivity, because the bill side is already locked in. The Public Utilities Board finalized a 4 per cent general rate increase effective January 1, 2026, with further increases of 3.5 per cent in 2027 and 3 per cent in 2028, framed as front-loading revenue to respond to drought impacts on hydroelectric generation. Manitoba Hydro is on the watch list this week for that reason: rates are settled through 2028, but the gas-versus-wind fight over how the utility grows past that point is still live and unresolved.

Zoom out to the national picture. Prime Minister Mark Carney opened his first Investment Summit in Toronto on Monday, pitching global investors on Canada, according to Canada's National Observer. Clean Energy Canada used the moment to make its own point. The group's program manager said the deal book released last week showcases Canada's potential to become a clean energy superpower while highlighting a gap between ambition and the money actually moving. Worth raising with clients who hold Canadian infrastructure or utility names: the ambition is loud right now, the capital commitments are still catching up.

Meanwhile in Alberta, Premier Danielle Smith said this weekend it's unlikely her government will launch a new Crown corporation to build gas pipelines, after a report on the idea leaked, per Canada's National Observer. So in one week you've got Manitoba's utility leaning into gas at the generation level, Alberta backing away from a state-run gas pipeline vehicle, and Ottawa trying to sell the country as a clean electricity destination, all pulling in slightly different directions.

On the charitable side, United Way Winnipeg closed its 2025 campaign with a record result. The organization says Winnipeggers raised a record-breaking $23.3 million for United Way Winnipeg's 2025 campaign, and it has named Anne Mahon, Chancellor Emeritus of the University of Manitoba, and Paul Mahon, former President and CEO of Canada Life, as co-chairs of the 2026 campaign. United Way Winnipeg is on the watch list this week for that reason.

For governance conversations with nonprofit board clients, here's a useful benchmark: United Way Winnipeg is accredited by Imagine Canada's Standards Program, a set of 73 standards that ensure effective, accountable, and ethical practices in nonprofit governance and management. That's a concrete, third-party standard you can point clients toward when they're vetting a charity's board practices before a major gift or a board seat, rather than relying on a glossy annual report alone.
talkingPoints: Manitoba Hydro's gas expansion plan just cleared six weeks of hostile hearings, worth flagging for utility-exposed holdings.
Hydro rates are locked through 2028 at 4, 3.5, and 3 percent, so build that into retiree cash flow planning now.
Ottawa's investment summit is heavy on clean energy talk, but Clean Energy Canada says the capital isn't matching the ambition yet.
Alberta just stepped back from a state-run gas pipeline company, a sign provinces are still feeling out the right structure.
United Way Winnipeg's $23.3 million record campaign and its Imagine Canada accreditation are a solid governance reference point for nonprofit clients.

blocks.label: AI & Technology
blocks.title: Anthropic's Slowdown Call Meets Wall Street Money
blocks.script:
The biggest story this week is Dario Amodei's essay calling for the industry to pace the frontier. The Anthropic chief executive published a thirty eight hundred word piece on Saturday arguing that development of the most advanced AI systems needs to slow down to avoid losing control of them. What makes this notable is who signed on: OpenAI's Sam Altman and Elon Musk's SpaceXAI both endorsed it. Bloomberg reports that Anthropic and OpenAI will have to weigh this against forces in the tech industry, financial markets, and the Trump administration that are likely to resist any real slowdown, especially with both companies eyeing potentially record setting initial public offerings that depend on continued frontier breakthroughs. Amodei insists pacing doesn't mean less spending or growth, but that's a hard sell to investors betting on hundreds of billions in capital expenditure.

Worth knowing for client conversations: President Trump publicly downplayed these risk warnings, per the BBC, framing them as negative forces raising concerns about things that won't happen, and tying it to competition with China. On the other side, Barack Obama told Democrats this week, according to TechCrunch, that AI needs to become a central agenda item with a clear plan on economic impact and safety. So you've got a real partisan split forming on how this gets regulated, which matters if you're advising anyone with exposure to AI infrastructure names.

There's also a useful counter frame here. Researchers Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor argue AI should be treated as a normal technology, not an incomprehensible superintelligence in waiting, and that view is gaining traction as a check on the doom messaging. BetaKit's newsletter this week flagged the AI bubble red flags directly: circular financing arrangements between chip makers, cloud providers, and model companies, plus concerns about rogue agentic tools operating with too little oversight. That's the kind of structural risk worth mentioning if a client asks why you're not chasing every AI headline into their portfolio.

On the Canadian side, BetaKit also reports Canada and Ukraine have struck a binational deal tapping Canadian drone companies, with firms from New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, and Saskatchewan receiving contracts. That's a real, if narrow, data point on where Canadian tech dollars and government procurement are actually flowing right now, defence and dual use tech rather than pure consumer AI.

Now the part that touches your clients directly. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre's 2025 figures show Canadians lost a record seven hundred four million dollars to fraud last year, up from six hundred forty five million in 2024, with investment fraud alone accounting for three hundred fifty one million of that. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security has separately warned that AI is shrinking the time defenders have to respond to attacks, from days down to hours, because generative tools let scammers write convincing phishing emails and voice clones at scale. If you haven't already, this is the week to remind clients that a phone call sounding exactly like a family member asking for a wire transfer is not proof of anything.

One item for the watch list: the Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at two and a quarter percent at its September second decision, the seventh straight hold, citing energy prices tied to the Middle East conflict and fresh trade tension with Washington. The next decision is October twenty eighth, and Governor Tiff Macklem's language suggests no clear signal either way until then.

Net for you: the AI story right now isn't about a new model release, it's about who controls the pace of the next one, and whether regulation lands before or after the capital keeps flowing.

Trump and Obama are on opposite sides of how hard to regulate AI, which will shape the policy risk in AI-heavy portfolios.
Canadian fraud losses hit a record seven hundred four million dollars last year, with investment scams the single largest category.
Ottawa's cyber centre says AI is cutting response time for defenders from days to hours, so verify any urgent money request by a second channel.
The Bank of Canada held rates again on September second, seventh straight hold, next decision October twenty eighth.

blocks.label: Health & Fitness
blocks.title: Strength Training Longevity Data, Creatine, and RSV Gaps
blocks.script:
The biggest health story this week comes from Harvard's T.H. Chan School of Public Health, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine. The study looked at three decades' worth of data from nearly 150,000 adults participating in three long-running studies, the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study, the Nurses' Health Study, and the Nurses' Health Study II. Roughly 90-120 minutes of strength training per week was linked with a 13% reduced risk of premature death, according to the study. Adults who averaged that range of weekly resistance training had a 13% lower risk of early death from any cause, a 19% lower risk from heart disease specifically. Adding aerobic exercise to the weekly mix increased the longevity benefit further. This is a long-running observational study, not a randomized trial, so it shows association, not proof of cause. But the sample size and three decades of tracking make it one of the stronger pieces of evidence yet that lifting does real work for longevity, not just muscle. The takeaway for someone who already lifts twice a week is that you're already in the zone where the data show the biggest return. No need to chase more volume for longevity's sake.

On the supplement side, Examine.com published a summary this year of a meta-analysis of 61 randomized controlled trials in 1,457 participants, finding that creatine combined with resistance training increased fat-free mass equally well in both trained and untrained lifters. So if you've been putting off creatine because you thought it was only for advanced lifters, the evidence doesn't back that up.

For the mobility side of training, Outside magazine published five yoga-inspired exercises for feet, ankles, and calves, aimed at people who hike or run outdoors. The logic holds in the gym too: weak ankle stability shows up as wobble under a loaded squat or lunge, and a few minutes of targeted foot and ankle work before a session is cheap insurance against rolled ankles and shifted form.

On the Canadian health system side, CBC reports that Nova Scotia's RSV, that's respiratory syncytial virus, vaccination program only covers three specific groups for free, leaving some seniors and immunocompromised people to pay out of pocket, a few hundred dollars per dose. It's a reminder that provincial vaccine coverage varies a lot across the country, worth checking directly with Manitoba Health if clients ask about their own eligibility this fall.

Two lifting sessions a week already puts you in the sweet spot for the longevity benefit.

A few minutes of ankle and foot mobility work protects your squat and lunge form.

blocks.label: Parenting
blocks.title: Canada Child Benefit Rises, Screen Time Guidance Holds Firm
blocks.script:
The biggest line for parents this year is a bank account, not a diagnosis. The Canada Child Benefit reset its payments in July, and Ottawa confirmed the new maximums this summer: up to eight thousand one hundred fifty seven dollars a year for a child under six, and up to six thousand eight hundred eighty three dollars for a child six to seventeen. That is an increase of up to $160 per child under age 6 and up to $135 per child aged 6 to 17 compared to the previous year. A family with one child aged 5 and one aged 9, with adjusted family net income of $65,000, will receive approximately $11,430 in 2026 to 27, nearly $400 more than the year before. The benefit has been indexed to inflation every year since 2018, so this is predictable, not a one off top up. For clients, that is real monthly cash flow worth revisiting, especially the question of whether some of it should flow straight into a Registered Education Savings Plan, or RESP, to capture the matching Canada Education Savings Grant.

On the paediatric side, guidance has not shifted this month. Canadian guidelines recommend no screen time for children under two, and for children two to five, routine or sedentary screen time limited to one hour or less per day. Canadian Paediatric Society principles still centre on minimizing, mitigating, mindfully using, and modelling healthy screen use rather than a strict stopwatch.

Separately, the Globe and Mail has a piece today on breakfast and school focus, citing evidence that a nutritious morning meal helps kids think and learn better in the classroom. Small, practical, consistent with what paediatric nutrition guidance has said for years, and worth passing along to clients juggling early drop offs.
talkingPoints: The CCB just went up, up to $160 more per child under six this year.
That extra cash flow is a good prompt to revisit RESP contributions and the grant match.
Screen guidance hasn't changed: none under two, about an hour through preschool.
Nutrition research keeps linking a solid breakfast to classroom focus.
Family benefit planning and education savings go hand in hand this fall.

blocks.label: Sports
blocks.title: Bombers Survive, Jets Camp Looms, Hellebuyck Watch
blocks.script:
The Winnipeg Blue Bombers beat the Saskatchewan Roughriders 19 to 6 in the Banjo Bowl on Saturday at Princess Auto Stadium. That puts them at 7 and 6, back in the thick of the West Division playoff race, per the Globe and Mail. The real story out of that game is quarterback Zach Collaros. He left in the third quarter with an undisclosed upper body injury after taking a beating, four of Saskatchewan's five sacks landed on him, and he finished 13 for 19 for 175 yards, a touchdown and two interceptions before backup Dru Brown closed it out, 4 for 5 for 46 yards, per CBC. Safety Redha Kramdi, back from a six game stretch on the injured list with a broken hand, forced a fumble and sealed the win with a fourth quarter interception. The Bombers are on their bye this week and return September 25th hosting the Toronto Argonauts. Watch for a Collaros update before then. Both the Bombers and the Jets are on your watch list, so this is a two team morning.

On the Jets, training camp opens Thursday at Hockey For All Centre. Preseason starts September 19th in Edmonton against the Oilers, then two home dates at Canada Life Centre, Colorado on the 21st and the Oilers again on the 22nd. The regular season is tentatively pegged for September 29th at home. The story hanging over camp is goaltender Connor Hellebuyck. He has requested a trade and has stayed off the ice at informal skates in Winnipeg. Captain Adam Lowry says the speculation is not worth the team's time, and Mark Scheifele says he still believes in this group coming off a career year of his own. If it is not resolved before the opener, expect it to follow the team on the road, and expect it to come up at every dinner table in the city.

Elsewhere in the NHL, new Maple Leafs general manager Chayka told the Globe and Mail he understands the weight of running the team he cheered for as a kid, after Toronto missed the playoffs last season for the first time since 2016. In Montreal, the Canadiens signed forward Zachary Bolduc to a four year extension, per CBC.

In the NFL, Sunday delivered the highest scoring season opener in league history as the Bears beat the Panthers, per the Globe and Mail. Kirk Cousins threw three touchdowns and joined the 300 touchdown club as the Raiders beat the Dolphins 27 to 13. Detroit escaped New Orleans in overtime, 31 to 30, with Jahmyr Gibbs putting up a career high 29 carries for 156 yards and two touchdowns. Buffalo got a late touchdown from Josh Allen to Joshua Palmer to beat Houston, their first win there since 2006. On the injury side, the reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year, Myles Garrett, needs knee surgery and is headed to injured reserve, out at least four games, per The Athletic.

In the NBA, Clippers owner Steve Ballmer said this weekend his team will accept the league's penalties for circumventing the salary cap to funnel money to Kawhi Leonard. He called it sincere regrets in a statement, per The Athletic.

Tonight closes out week one of the NFL with Monday Night Football. The CFL is quiet with the Bombers on their bye, and the NBA stays in the off season while Jets camp opens in three days.

Zach Collaros left hurt again, watch for word before the September 25th Argos game.

Kirk Cousins just joined the NFL's 300 touchdown club with Las Vegas.
Clippers owner Steve Ballmer is accepting the cap circumvention penalties tied to Kawhi Leonard.

blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: SPIVA: how active managers have done against benchmarks, by category and horizon / FHSA: eligibility, room, and how it stacks with the RRSP Home Buyers Plan / Framing: how the first sentence sets the frame for everything after
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Evidence arsenal, lesson 2: SPIVA: how active managers have done against benchmarks, by category and horizon.

Here is the number that should end most debates about picking a stock picker. In the SPIVA U.S. Year-End 2024 scorecard from S&P Dow Jones Indices, sixty-five percent of large-cap core active funds underperformed the S&P 500 in 2024 alone. Stretch the horizon to ten years and eighty-four percent underperformed. Stretch it to twenty years and it is eighty-seven percent. That is not one bad year. That is the base rate.

SPIVA works by comparing active fund returns, net of fees, against the matching benchmark, and it corrects for survivorship bias, meaning it counts funds that closed or merged away, not just the survivors bragging on their own website. It breaks results out by category: large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap, international, fixed income, and by horizon: one year, three, five, ten, fifteen, twenty. The pattern holds across almost every slice. Small-cap managers do marginally better some years, emerging markets sometimes too, but the multi-year numbers converge toward the same conclusion: most active managers, most of the time, do not beat their benchmark after fees.

The one mistake people make is reading a single strong one-year number and treating it as skill. If forty percent of large-cap managers beat the index in a given year, roughly half the field beats the index in any coin-flip year. The evidence that matters is the ten and fifteen year window, because that is long enough to separate luck from a repeatable edge, and even there the odds stack against active management.

What this technique reveals is a probability, category by category, against the appropriate benchmark. What it cannot tell you is which specific manager, if any, will be in that surviving minority going forward. That question is a different lesson.

For today, pull the SPIVA scorecard for one category relevant to a client's actual holdings, S&P 500 or S&P MidCap 400 for example, and write down the one-year, five-year, and ten-year underperformance percentages. If you want a cross-check on Thomson ONE, the fund screener's category peer rankings will show you the same underperformance pattern against the benchmark column.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 5: FHSA: eligibility, room, and how it stacks with the RRSP Home Buyers Plan.

The First Home Savings Account, or FHSA, is the one account that gives you an RRSP-style deduction going in and a TFSA-style tax-free withdrawal coming out, as long as the money buys a first home. For 2026, the annual contribution limit is 8,000 dollars, the lifetime limit is 40,000 dollars, and unused room carries forward one year at a time, up to 8,000 dollars extra. To open one, your client needs to be a Canadian resident, at least 18 in Manitoba, and a first-time buyer, meaning they or their spouse haven't owned and lived in a home in the current calendar year or the four before it. The account has to be collapsed within 15 years of opening, or by age 71, whichever comes first.

Here's the stacking piece advisors get wrong. Say a client opened an FHSA in 2023 and contributed 8,000 a year through 2026, that's 32,000 dollars, fully deducted against income each year. When they buy their first home, they withdraw that 32,000 completely tax-free, no repayment required, unlike the Home Buyers' Plan. Then, on the same purchase, they can also pull from their RRSP under the Home Buyers' Plan. The HBP limit was raised to 60,000 dollars per person, up from 35,000, for withdrawals made after April 16, 2024, per the federal budget that year. So a couple could combine two FHSAs and two HBP withdrawals and bring well over 180,000 dollars to a down payment, all pulled from registered accounts, all tax-sheltered on the way in or the way out.

The mistake people make is assuming FHSA withdrawals get repaid like HBP withdrawals. They don't. FHSA money used for a qualifying purchase is gone tax-free, permanently, no 15-year repayment schedule. Clients confuse the two and think they owe the account money later. They don't, HBP does, FHSA doesn't.

Communication, lesson 4: Framing: how the first sentence sets the frame for everything after.

In 1981, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman ran an experiment now called the Asian disease problem. They gave people the same crisis, 600 people at risk, and two mathematically identical outcomes worded differently. One group heard "Program A saves 200 lives." 72% chose it. Another group heard the identical option worded as "400 people will die." Only 22% chose it. Same 600 people, same math, same outcome. The only variable was the first frame: lives saved versus lives lost. The opening sentence doesn't just describe reality, it tells the listener which reality to feel.

Put that in your client meeting. A client's portfolio is down 12% this quarter against the S&P 500's 8% drop over the same period, per the fund's own filing. You could open with "Your portfolio dropped 12% this quarter." Or you could open with "Your portfolio held up better than the index by 4 points, and here's what that protection is worth over ten years." Same numbers. Completely different frame. The first sentence decides whether the client hears loss or context.

The mistake most advisors make is leading with the apology. "I know this hasn't been our best quarter" sets the frame as "bad news is coming," and everything after gets filtered through worry, no matter how strong the follow-up data is.

Here's your task, under fifteen minutes. Take one piece of news you owe someone this week, a number, a delay, a result. Write two opening sentences for it. One framed around risk. One framed around progress or direction. Read both aloud and notice which one you'd want to hear if you were the client.

For your drill: record yourself opening three different messages, thirty seconds each. Score each first sentence on one thing only, does it name a direction, up, down, or on track, within the first seven words. Two out of three passes counts as a pass overall.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull one client file with an RRSP balance and no FHSA, calculate their combined FHSA plus HBP capacity if they opened an FHSA today, and write the number down.

Communication: Take one piece of news you owe someone this week and write two opening sentences for it, one framed around risk and one framed around progress, then read both aloud to compare how each lands.

Here's your task, under fifteen minutes. Take one piece of news you owe someone this week, a number, a delay, a result. Write two opening sentences for it. One framed around risk. One framed around progress or direction. Read both aloud and notice which one you'd want to hear if you were the client.

For your drill: record yourself opening three different messages, thirty seconds each. Score each first sentence on one thing only, does it name a direction, up, down, or on track, within the first seven words. Two out of three passes counts as a pass overall.
lessons.task: Take one piece of news you owe someone this week and write two opening sentences for it, one framed around risk and one framed around progress, then read both aloud to compare how each lands.
lessons.drill: Record three separate thirty second message openings. Score each first sentence pass or fail on whether it names a clear direction (up, down, on track, ahead, behind) within the first seven words. Good looks like two out of three passing, with the direction word appearing before any caveat, apology, or background detail.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Oil Spike, Bond Selloff, Bank of Canada Holds Steady
blocks.script:
Start with oil, because it is driving almost everything else you will hear about in markets today. Brent crude is trading above one hundred dollars a barrel this morning, touching close to one hundred and two dollars, after Iran and the United States traded their largest wave of attacks on shipping since their conflict began roughly six months ago. Iran hit vessels near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. struck Iranian oil tankers, and tanker freight rates have jumped to record levels as shippers and insurers price in the risk of moving crude through that corridor. West Texas Intermediate, the North American benchmark, is trading in the high nineties, up close to one and a half percent on the day. For clients, the direct read is at the pump and in the next inflation print. Higher energy costs feed straight into headline inflation, which is exactly why the European Central Bank raised its policy rate by twenty five basis points yesterday, its second hike since the Iran war began, even as it lifted its own inflation outlook for the euro area.

Closer to home, the TSX, the Toronto Stock Exchange, fell for a third straight session yesterday, down about six tenths of a percent to just under thirty five thousand nine hundred. Shopify was a big drag, falling another five point four percent after an already rough prior session. South of the border, the S&P 500 slipped about half a percent, the Dow fell just over three quarters of a percent, and the Nasdaq was off six tenths, all closing lower for a third straight day. Behind the equity weakness is the bond market. The U.S. ten year Treasury yield pushed to a fresh three year high near four point eight six percent, and that move actually came after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a bond buyback plan meant to push yields lower. The move backfired, yields rose instead of falling, and one bond manager put it bluntly, saying the market has effectively called his bluff. The takeaway for clients holding fixed income is that this is no longer just a Federal Reserve story, it is a fiscal credibility story, with the U.S. deficit and talk of a five thousand dollar per adult election year payout adding to the unease.

Here at home, the Bank of Canada rate decision is one I always want you tracking, and the headline is a hold. The Bank of Canada's latest announcement, made on September 2nd, was a policy interest rate hold for a seventh consecutive time, keeping the rate at 2.25%. It described the recovery as broadening, pointing to second-quarter GDP growth of 3.3%, solid consumer spending, a rebound in housing activity, and sharp gains in exports and business investment. Statistics Canada's own dashboard has the unemployment rate at 6.4% for August and CPI, the Consumer Price Index, at 3.0% for July, so inflation is still running a full point above target while the labour market has softened. That combination is exactly why the Bank is on hold rather than cutting. The next scheduled date for announcing the overnight rate target is October 28, 2026, and it lands with a fresh Monetary Policy Report, so that is the date to circle for clients asking when things might change.

The loonie is weaker on all of this, trading around seventy two point four cents U.S., down about two tenths of a percent on the day, even though it is still up close to nine tenths of a percent over the past month. A softer dollar alongside triple digit oil is an unusual mix for Canada, normally rising crude supports the loonie given our export exposure, but right now safe haven demand for the U.S. dollar and the geopolitical risk premium are winning out.

On trade, the picture is more nuanced than the headlines suggest. Kirsten Hillman, Canada's former ambassador to Washington, told the Globe and Mail that formal negotiations with the U.S. could be months away because Ottawa is holding firm on its auto, steel, and aluminum red lines. The Globe's own numbers show the latest American tariff expansion added less than half a percentage point to the total value of Canadian goods covered, so the macro damage looks contained, though economist Stephen Brown at Capital Economics still expects Canadian GDP could contract in the third quarter. The real pain is concentrated in specific sectors: furniture, dairy, and wood products face new punitive tariffs, Canadian motorcycles are banned from crossing the border starting September twenty ninth, and so is packaged alcohol, including canned beer and rye whisky, though bulk shipments can still cross for bottling stateside. If you have clients exposed to those specific industries, that is where the conversation needs to go, not a broad portfolio panic.

On housing, two Canadian data points worth having ready for clients. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the federal housing agency, says the country still needs between four hundred seventeen thousand and four hundred sixty nine thousand new housing units a year to restore affordability, and it is warning the pace of construction could actually slow from here. Separately, the Bank of Canada's own affordability index, which weighs housing costs against disposable income, still sits well above its long run normal level. Prices have come down from the peak but not enough to call the affordability problem fixed, and that matters directly for anyone in Winnipeg thinking about a mortgage renewal into a rate environment that looks stuck at two and a quarter percent through year end.

On the fiscal and investment side, Prime Minister Mark Carney's Canada Investment Summit has a prospectus circulating with more than one hundred sixty projects looking for capital. Two figures stand out: a ten point nine billion dollar high speed rail link between Edmonton and Calgary, and a fifty seven billion dollar expansion of the Port of Churchill, right here in Manitoba. Worth flagging to clients that foreign capital is genuinely flowing into Canada right now, though closer reporting shows it is largely a U.S. driven boom rather than a truly diversified global one, so do not oversell the diversification story yet.

Finally, on earnings, Oracle and Adobe both beat estimates after the bell, with Oracle's cloud and artificial intelligence infrastructure demand coming in ahead of expectations and Adobe posting adjusted profit of six dollars and thirteen cents a share against a six-oh-nine estimate. That matters because Oracle has been the poster child for anxiety over AI financing, its stock down roughly half over the past year with the cost of credit protection up more than forty percent, so a beat here takes some heat off the broader AI trade, at least for today. Worth mentioning to any client with technology exposure that the sector is still highly binary on execution.
talkingPoints: Oil above one hundred dollars a barrel is the story behind higher inflation risk and this week's bond selloff.
The Bank of Canada held at two and a quarter percent for a seventh straight meeting, next decision is October twenty eighth.
The loonie is softer even with oil this high, safe haven demand for U.S. dollars is overriding the usual pattern.
New U.S. tariffs hit specific sectors hard, furniture, dairy, motorcycles, and packaged alcohol, but the broad economic hit looks contained.
CMHC says Canada still needs four hundred seventeen to four hundred sixty nine thousand new homes a year, affordability is not fixed yet.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Oracle, Anthropic, Shopify Lead Today's Watchlist
blocks.script:
Start with your watch list. The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at two point two five percent this month, the seventh straight hold, with governor Tiff Macklem citing high energy prices from the Iran conflict and fresh uncertainty from new United States tariffs and Canadian countermeasures. The tailwind is a stronger than expected second quarter that gave the bank room to pause. The headwind is oil trading near one hundred dollars a barrel and a bond selloff pushing borrowing costs higher no matter what Ottawa does. An evidence based advisor tells you not to reposition a portfolio around one rate hold, keep your mix diversified, and let the bank's own data drive changes, not headlines.

Oracle is the enterprise software and cloud company that now builds much of the computing power behind artificial intelligence. Shares rose in premarket trading Friday after fiscal first quarter results beat estimates, with the Globe and Mail reporting the AI boom is boosting cloud demand. The tailwind is a contract backlog that Reuters says climbed past six hundred billion dollars. The headwind is the debt load funding that buildout, with Bloomberg noting the cost of insuring Oracle's debt against default has risen more than forty percent this year. An evidence based advisor says this is a single stock bet on one theme, size it small if you own it at all, and let a broad index carry the AI exposure instead.

Anthropic is the artificial intelligence lab behind the Claude models, and it is the company everyone in tech is arguing about right now. A researcher named Jacob Coxon resigned this week warning, as the Peak reports, that people building the technology believe it could kill us all by decade's end, and colleagues Evan Hubinger and Samuel Marks echoed the concern. Separately, the Globe and Mail reports Anthropic says it blocked misuse of its models tied to biological weapons, and United States lawmakers are now pushing new rules. The tailwind is real demand and Washington attention. The headwind is safety warnings from its own staff. An evidence based advisor says don't trade your portfolio on a single company's internal alarm, that's a policy story, not a valuation one.

Adobe makes the software behind Photoshop and much of professional publishing, and it just reported mixed signals in one day. The Globe and Mail says Adobe beat Wall Street's profit estimate at six dollars and thirteen cents a share, yet Bloomberg reports its forecast missed expectations, reviving fears that generative AI tools built by competitors are eating into demand for its own products. The tailwind is still solid current earnings. The headwind is a guidance number that spooked traders. An evidence based advisor tells a client that one guidance miss doesn't break a long term thesis, but it's a reminder that AI disruption cuts both ways for incumbents.

Shopify is the Ottawa built e-commerce platform that powers online stores worldwide. Its shares fell five point four percent yesterday after dropping seven point eight percent the day before, the Peak reports, as broader market jitters over bond yields and tariff uncertainty hit growth stocks hardest. The tailwind is that this looks like a market wide selloff, not a company specific problem. The headwind is that high growth, high valuation names like Shopify get hit hardest when yields rise and risk appetite fades. An evidence based advisor says a two day drop tells you nothing new about the business, check the fundamentals before you touch the position.

Nvidia designs the chips that power most of the world's artificial intelligence data centres. Bloomberg reports the Department of Justice is investigating whether Nvidia structured its twenty billion dollar licensing deal with chip startup Groq to dodge antitrust review. The tailwind is Nvidia's continued dominance of the AI chip market and steady demand from every major cloud buyer. The headwind is regulatory risk that could reshape how it strikes future deals. An evidence based advisor says antitrust probes take years and rarely move a stock on headlines alone, so don't sell a core holding over an investigation announcement.

CIBC is one of Canada's big five banks. It just committed two billion dollars over five years to finance defence related companies, the Globe and Mail reports, covering sectors from infrastructure to energy deemed critical to the economy. The tailwind is Ottawa's broader push to rearm and rebuild domestic industry, which hands banks a new lending category. The headwind is execution risk in a sector Canadian banks have limited history underwriting at scale. An evidence based advisor says bank stocks remain a reasonable core holding for income and stability, but don't buy CIBC specifically because of one lending program.

BMO, another of the big five, shows up twice today. The Peak's headline flags BMO going after challenger banks, and separately a BMO analyst tells the Globe and Mail that infrastructure investment could supercharge Canada's mining sector ahead of next week's investment summit. The tailwind is BMO positioning itself across both retail banking competition and resource sector financing. The headwind is that both stories are strategy commentary, not results. An evidence based advisor says Canadian banks are well capitalized and diversified by design, hold them as part of a broad portfolio rather than chasing a single headline.

Enbridge operates the pipeline network moving oil and gas across North America, including the aging Line 5. Michigan regulators are reviewing tunnel permits for a Line 5 replacement while Governor Gretchen Whitmer calls the pipeline a ticking time bomb, per the Globe and Mail. The tailwind is steady demand for pipeline capacity as North American energy prices climb. The headwind is years of regulatory and political risk in Michigan that could delay or kill the tunnel project. An evidence based advisor says regulatory fights like this can drag on for a decade, price patience into any position, not a quick resolution.

Apple just showed the world its first folding iPhone. The Peak reports chief executive officer John Ternus unveiled the iPhone Duo, with a seven point six inch unfolded screen, Apple's biggest design shift since the iPad, priced around two thousand seven hundred and fifty dollars with preorders starting October sixteenth. The tailwind is a genuine new product category to reignite upgrade demand. The headwind is a price point that limits it to a small slice of buyers early on. An evidence based advisor says a single product launch, however dramatic, rarely justifies changing a long term position in a company this size.
talkingPoints: The Bank of Canada held rates again, don't expect a cut soon.
Oracle's earnings beat eased some fear about its AI debt load.
Anthropic's own staff are the ones sounding the loudest alarm now.
Shopify's slide looks like a market wide move, not a company problem.
Canada's big banks keep leaning into defence and resource financing.

blocks.label: Practice: Tax, Regulatory & Industry
blocks.title: Cap Gains Whipsaw, Manitoba Budget, CIRO CE Rules
blocks.script:
The biggest read for incorporated business owners today comes out of Ottawa, not Manitoba. Advisor.ca reports federal coffers were boosted in 2024 by taxpayers triggering capital gains ahead of the capital gains inclusion rate hike that Ottawa ultimately scrapped. Investment Executive frames it the same way, a short-term revenue gain from a proposal that never became law still came with real costs to the people who acted on it. If you have clients who crystallized gains personally or inside a holding company in 2024, anticipating a two-thirds inclusion rate, this is the receipt. Ottawa collected more, then walked the policy back. For Canadian-controlled private corporation owners sitting on passive investment portfolios inside the company, the passive income rules themselves haven't moved this week. The lesson is about process: don't restructure a holdco or trigger gains based on a proposal before it has royal assent. Wait for the legislation, not the headline.

Closer to home, Manitoba's own tax picture is settled for now. The 2026 provincial budget, tabled in March by Finance Minister Adrien Sala, made no changes to personal or corporate income tax rates, and left the five hundred thousand dollar small business limit untouched. What did move: the province is removing the seven percent retail sales tax on more grocery store food and beverages, and it's bringing in land transfer tax anti-avoidance amendments aimed at property transactions structured to dodge the tax, effective January 1, 2027. If you have clients doing corporate reorganizations touching Manitoba real property, or a physician buying into a clinic building, flag that land transfer change now, not in December 2026.

On the regulatory side, CIRO, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, is deep into harmonizing continuing education rules across the old investment dealer and mutual fund dealer channels. Investment Executive's commentary today digs into the fine print. The proposed rule sets different minimum assessment requirements depending on who delivers the course, a dealer-run session needs a built-in knowledge check, an externally delivered one doesn't have to prove it has one. Comments closed in July, and CIRO is aiming to publish final rules in the second half of 2027, with the harmonized regime starting January 1, 2028. That's a practice management item for your own licensing file, not a client conversation, but worth knowing before compliance starts asking what you did this cycle.

The Ontario Securities Commission has named the members of its new Capital Markets Advisory Committee, a one-year pilot announced back in April, with its first meeting this month. It's stacked with senior industry names, from BlackRock Canada's Margaret Gunawan to IGM Financial's Rhonda Goldberg, and it replaces input that used to flow through two separate committees now paused for the pilot. Not a client-meeting story, but it tells you where rule-making priorities get shaped over the next year.

On the RRSP file, a financial markets industry group has put a pre-budget submission to Finance Canada asking Ottawa to let Canadians hold Registered Retirement Savings Plans intact until age 74, up from the current mandatory conversion at 71, and to lift annual contribution room to fifty-six thousand three hundred fifty dollars, with registered plans opened to private equity and venture capital funds. None of that is law, it's an ask. If you have clients approaching 71 this year or next, plan on today's rules and revisit if this actually moves.

On product and fees, Bank of Montreal has become the first of the big five banks to eliminate most online trading commissions at BMO InvestorLine, matching the discount brokerage price war that's been building all year. Manulife updated the status of nineteen segregated funds in one announcement, eight new, eleven gaining wider series access across GIF Select, the segregated fund RESP, and the MPIP pools. If you use segregated funds for creditor protection with incorporated professional clients, physicians and dentists especially, check whether a mandate you rely on just picked up a lower-cost series.

The trade file keeps landing on small business owners specifically. Wealth Professional cites new Canadian Federation of Independent Business data putting more than fifty-three thousand small businesses at risk from the latest American import bans, hitting furniture, dairy, and wood products, plus Canadian-made motorcycles and canned or bottled alcohol including rye whisky, starting September 29. If you have an incorporated client exporting into the U.S. in any of those categories, this is a cash flow and valuation conversation this month, not next quarter.

Last one, and it touches life transition planning directly. Globe Advisor covers a new Capgemini and LIMRA report finding many younger clients discontinue life insurance within three years of buying a policy. The same newsletter's piece on longevity planning quotes advisor Brad Smith saying credentials are just the tip of the iceberg, listening to what's changing in a client's life matters more than the plan on paper. If you have clients newly incorporated, newly divorced, or newly parents, that's exactly when insurance lapses happen, and it's the moment to check in before a policy quietly ends.
talkingPoints: Ottawa's 2024 capital gains bump was real but temporary, don't act on policy before royal assent.
Manitoba's tax rates and small business limit are unchanged for 2026, but the land transfer tax anti-avoidance rule lands January 2027.
CIRO's continuing education harmonization won't bite until 2028, but assessment standards already differ by who delivers the course.
BMO just went fee-free on online trading, expect the other bank platforms to respond.
Check life insurance in force for any client mid-transition, incorporation, divorce, new baby, lapse risk peaks in year one to three.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Judges, Doctors, Hydro, and a Rate Hold
blocks.script:
Start with the story that has lawyers and judges rattled. Manitoba's provincial court is cutting sittings because there aren't enough judges to keep the schedule running. The Free Press reports the court is slashing 68 annual sittings across nine rural circuit locations and at St. Boniface, effective April 2027. Chief Judge Ryan Rolston signed the notice, citing what he called huge resource gaps between the caseload and the number of judges available. Lawyers quoted in the paper worry this erodes public confidence in the justice system, and the Free Press's own opinion page ran a piece titled "cancelling court erodes access to justice." If you sit on any board dealing with commercial litigation or estate disputes, expect longer waits.

Health care is the other big one. Premier Wab Kinew is now musing publicly about pulling lab services back into the public system, after the labour dispute with Dynacare, the private lab contractor, has dragged on. The union representing the striking workers says Kinew is engaged in what it calls damage control, not a real fix. Meanwhile Dynacare's own chief medical officer told CBC that Manitoba hospitals don't always have the capacity to handle their own testing, which is part of why the province leaned on a private contractor in the first place.

On doctors, there's a good news, bad news split. Manitoba gained physicians for a third straight year, which a physicians' advocacy group calls a record pace of recruitment. But the same report says the province is losing doctors at a rate not seen since the depths of the COVID pandemic, and CBC notes the losses are concentrated in the western region. So the net number looks fine, the regional distribution does not.

Manitoba Hydro is on the watch list, and it came up today. Free Press staff report the premier is downplaying concerns about leadership turnover at Hydro, saying it is not a concern. Given the Crown utility's track record of board and executive shakeups over the past couple of years, that's a line worth remembering if a client asks about rate stability.

On the trade file, the Manitoba government unveiled a new Manitoba Canada Defence Alliance this week, essentially a push to capture a bigger share of national defence spending for the province. That comes as the U.S. rolled out fresh import bans hitting Canadian alcohol, whey, and motorcycles, part of an escalating trade war. The Canadian Press reports economists don't expect this round of tariffs to meaningfully dent near-term Canadian growth, though a small business advocacy group here says the next few months are critical for Manitoba firms feeling the squeeze.

Since a client will ask, the Bank of Canada is also on your watch list. It held its overnight rate at 2.25 percent on September 2nd, the seventh straight hold, with the bank rate at 2.5 percent. The bank flagged stronger upside risks to inflation from Middle East energy prices and the tariff fight, but said the economy had a broad recovery in the second quarter. Next decision is October 28th.

On the ground here, the City of Winnipeg has actually beaten its housing targets under the federal Housing Accelerator Fund, with permits issued for close to 14,900 new units since December 2023, clearing the bar needed to claim $126.5 million in federal money. Separately, more than 21,000 free youth transit passes have gone out under the province's new pilot, and the city has agreed to install full safety shields for transit drivers after the union pushed for it.

Sports, since it will come up at dinner. The Jets are on your watch list too, and training camp opens shortly with new faces Ferraro and Skinner getting oriented before puck drop. The Blue Bombers, also on your list, host the Banjo Bowl at Princess Auto Stadium Saturday, looking to avenge their overtime loss in Regina over the Labour Day weekend.
talkingPoints: Circuit court sittings are being cut province wide starting April 2027, expect slower timelines on litigation.
Kinew is now openly talking about bringing lab services back into the public system after the Dynacare dispute.
Manitoba is gaining doctors overall but losing them out west at a pace not seen since the pandemic.
Bank of Canada held its rate at 2.25 percent again, seventh straight hold, next decision October 28th.
Winnipeg beat its federal housing targets, clearing $126.5 million in Housing Accelerator funding.

blocks.label: Canadian Politics
blocks.title: Banff Retreat, Trade Fire, and a Manitoba Seaport Bet
blocks.script:
The biggest story this week is where the federal cabinet spent it: not in Ottawa, but in Banff, at what the government calls the Cabinet Planning Forum. Mark Carney and his ministers spent two days plotting the fall sitting of Parliament against two pressures at once, an escalating trade fight with the United States and an Alberta independence referendum that lands October 19th. CTV News reported that cabinet ministers were asked to show how they've advanced the government's seven stated priorities, and one of those, building a new economic and security relationship with the U.S., is the one that matters most for anyone with cross-border business.

On trade, the picture is more nuanced than the rhetoric suggests. The Globe and Mail's analysis found that the latest round of American tariffs pushed the value of Canadian goods affected under one U.S. statute to twenty point two six billion dollars, up from twenty point one five billion, an increase of less than half of one percent. Economist Stephen Brown of Capital Economics called it a soft jab rather than a hammer blow, though he warned Canadian gross domestic product could still contract in the third quarter. Carney himself has called the U.S. measures relatively modest and says he remains in regular contact with President Trump. But specific sectors are getting hit hard: motorcycles made in Canada are banned from crossing the border starting September 29th, and new tariffs are landing on furniture, dairy, wood products, and alcoholic beverages including canned beer and rye whisky. Former Canadian ambassador to Washington Kirsten Hillman told the Globe that formal trade talks may be months away, with Ottawa holding firm on red lines around the auto, steel, and aluminum sectors. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre spent the week in New York making the opposite case for urgency, telling American audiences that Canadians feel, in his words, wounded and confused at being targeted, according to CBC.

On the Alberta file, Carney has suggested Ottawa won't be bankrolling federalist campaign groups ahead of the referendum, citing provincial spending rules that strictly limit federal involvement, the Globe reports. Polls show separatist support is a minority position, but organizers on the pro-Canada side are described as cash-strapped and still finding their footing.

For your Manitoba clients, the one to watch is the federal investment summit happening in Toronto next week. CBC has obtained the government's prospectus, which lists 167 projects seeking capital, and among them is a fifty-seven billion dollar expansion of the Port of Churchill, Manitoba's Arctic seaport. That sits alongside a ten point nine billion dollar Edmonton to Calgary high-speed rail proposal. Whether Churchill investment actually materializes is the open question, but it's now formally part of Ottawa's pitch to investors.

On the Bank of Canada, which is on the watch list: the Bank held its policy rate at two point two five percent on September 2nd, the seventh consecutive hold, unchanged since last October's cut. The Bank flagged rising inflation risk from Middle East energy prices and the tariff fight, but gave no signal of a near-term move. The next decision lands October 28th.

Back home, the Manitoba legislature returns September 29th for its fall sitting, with Premier Wab Kinew's NDP government facing an opposition Progressive Conservative caucus led by Obby Khan.

One more item with a Prairie resonance: Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a hundred-year defence partnership in Calgary this week, centred on drone manufacturing, with Carney saying a third of all drones built in Canada will go to Ukraine's defence. The symbolism wasn't lost on anyone, given how deep Ukrainian roots run across the Prairies, Manitoba included.
talkingPoints: Tariff impact so far is described by economists as modest at the macro level, even as specific sectors face real pain.
The Port of Churchill's fifty-seven billion dollar expansion is now part of Ottawa's formal investment pitch, worth watching for Manitoba exposure.
The Bank of Canada held rates again, seventh straight hold, next decision October 28th.
Alberta's referendum is October 19th, and Ottawa says it won't fund the federalist side directly.

blocks.label: Climate Policy & Nonprofit Governance
blocks.title: Manitoba Hydro Gas Plan Faces Tough Hearings
blocks.script:
Manitoba Hydro's six weeks of public hearings into its energy expansion plan wrapped up this week, and CBC News reports the criticism only got louder toward the end. Intervenors, including the Public Interest Law Centre, told the Public Utilities Board there's no credible load forecast to justify Hydro's claim that it could run short of power by 2030, and they questioned whether the utility's three proposed natural gas turbines can really be built for three billion dollars. This is the plan to add one thousand, seven hundred and sixty additional megawatts, more than a quarter of Hydro's existing capacity, over the next decade, mixing new gas generation with a call for six hundred megawatts of wind power and expanded efficiency programs. The Public Utilities Board is weighing all this against a rate case that already has a four percent increase locked in on an interim basis as of January. Manitoba Hydro is on your watch list, and this is the fight that will decide whether power bills climb faster because of gas, or whether wind and efficiency carry more of the load. Worth flagging for clients who hold Hydro-related paper or who sit on municipal boards affected by rate decisions.

Ottawa is also in the news. Prime Minister Carney's cabinet wrapped a second day of closed-door meetings in Banff, preparing for the fall sitting of Parliament, per Canada's National Observer. The outlet's opinion desk also flagged that Ottawa released a damning report on the country's climate trajectory over a weekend, timing critics call a bid to bury bad news. For clients watching federal climate credibility ahead of budget season, that's a sign the fall fiscal update will get scrutinized hard on follow-through, not just announcements.

On the business side, a new survey covered by the National Observer finds nearly three-quarters of Canadian clean economy firms say they've already felt the sting of American tariffs, hitting different companies in very different ways. Sector leaders are asking Ottawa's fall budget to focus on competitiveness rather than more tariff relief. If you've got clients in cleantech manufacturing or supply chains, that's the ask to watch when the budget lands.

West of us, Alberta rolled out a fourteen-dollar recycling fee on every new solar panel starting October the first, and the National Observer reports industry groups still want to see the numbers behind that price. The paper also profiles a rural county where the tax base flipped from oil and gas to wind and solar over a decade, and now faces a budget hole because Alberta is reining in renewables even as unpaid oil and gas taxes pile up. Useful contrast for Manitoba clients: provinces are placing very different bets on where the energy dollars go.

On the charitable side, CanadaHelps recently summarized guidance from the CRA's Charities Directorate, and it's a good governance reminder for any client who sits on a board. Sharmila Khare, the Directorate's director general, noted most of the more than eighty-two thousand charity returns filed in a recent year had fixable problems, incomplete T3010 filings or disorganized records. But the Directorate also warned specifically against lending a charitable registration number to affiliates, and against inflated receipts for non-cash gifts that can't be substantiated. If you have clients who direct small charities, that's worth a direct check-in.

And United Way Winnipeg is on your watch list too. The organization is holding its 2026 Report to Community and annual general meeting, framed around the theme Meeting the Moment, alongside newer initiatives like a joint youth space in Portage la Prairie with the Manitoba government and Health Canada. Good context if donor clients ask where United Way dollars are landing this year.

blocks.label: AI & Technology
blocks.title: Apple Unveils Foldable iPhone as AI Safety Fears Grow
blocks.script:
Good morning. Here is your technology briefing for September 11th, 2026.

Apple has entered the foldable phone market with a new device called the iPhone Duo. According to reporting from Bloomberg, newly appointed Apple CEO John Ternus introduced the phone at a major event this week, taking a swipe at rival foldables by calling them, in his words, two phones awkwardly stuck together.

The Duo opens up to a nearly seven and a half inch screen, the largest ever on an iPhone, with a smaller outer display for use when folded. Apple says the hinge design reduces the crease that has been a common complaint about competing foldables, and the phone will support the Apple Pencil later this year.

Tech analyst Ben Thompson, writing in his Stratechery newsletter, said the launch shows Apple once again blending hardware and software tightly together, with iOS redesigned around the dual screens for multitasking and split view apps. He noted that companies like Zoom, Slack, and Netflix have already built custom features for the new device. Thompson pointed out the irony that Netflix, which refused to support Apple's Vision Pro headset, is now front and center for the Duo, a sign that developers work with Apple mainly out of self interest rather than loyalty.

On the AI industry side, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told TechCrunch he expects the company to grow around 70 percent next year, insisting that the flood of deals across the AI supply chain are not circular financial arrangements as some critics have suggested.

OpenAI has temporarily paused new sign-ups for its Pro subscription tier. TechCrunch reports the company says demand tied to its Astra product has strained its systems, and it is adding capacity before reopening subscriptions.

Meta's newest app, an AI agent called Muse, has climbed to the number two spot among apps in the United States, though TechCrunch notes its rollout has been slower than earlier Meta products like Threads.

On the safety front, Anthropic released a new threat intelligence report this week detailing what it calls persistent efforts by China-based AI firms, including Alibaba, Moonshot AI, and DeepSeek, to distill or copy its models, with the company saying these attempts have intensified as competition in the sector heats up.

Separately, the BBC reports Anthropic also disclosed that it blocked an apparent attempt to use its AI systems to help design biological weapons, and TechCrunch highlighted the company's findings on how rogue AI agents online can struggle with everyday obstacles like CAPTCHAs.

These safety disclosures are feeding into political pressure. The Globe and Mail reports that US lawmakers from both parties are increasingly calling for new AI regulation after a string of incidents involving rogue agents and the safety warnings from Anthropic researchers.

Finally, in the audio content space, India's Pocket FM told TechCrunch it has doubled its revenue run rate to 500 million dollars, crediting AI for producing the vast majority of its new audio content and cutting production costs dramatically.
talkingPoints: Apple bets its foldable can outclass rivals through tighter software integration, though critics note its app ecosystem still depends on third party goodwill.
Nvidia's growth forecast underscores continued confidence in AI infrastructure spending, even as scrutiny of circular deal structures persists.
Anthropic's twin disclosures on model distillation and bioweapons risk are accelerating bipartisan momentum in Washington for AI oversight.

blocks.label: Health & Fitness
blocks.title: Strength Training Data, Recall, and Wearable Bias
blocks.script:
The biggest health story this week for anyone who trains is a Harvard-led study just published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine. Researchers analyzed three major studies involving 147,374 adults who were middle-aged or older at the study's start and tracked for up to 30 years. They found that people who logged between 90 and 119 minutes of resistance training each week were 13% less likely to die during the study period from any cause compared with those who did no strength training. They also had a 19% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease and a 27% lower risk of dying from neurological diseases such as dementia. This is a large observational cohort, not a randomized trial, so it shows association rather than proof that lifting caused the difference, but the size and the multi-decade follow up make it one of the stronger looks we have at strength training and lifespan. The practical takeaway for your clients who lift: somewhere around two solid one-hour sessions a week appears to be the sweet spot, and aerobic exercise remained a strong, independent predictor of living longer, but the greatest benefit was observed when resistance training was combined with it.

On the Canadian side, Teva Canada is recalling a lot of 500-milligram Nov-Gesic Forte acetaminophen due to the potential presence of phenolic resin or epoxy, according to a Thursday news release from Health Canada. If ingested, this may cause injury to the digestive system. The affected batch carries Lot No. 100083040, with an expiration date of January 31, 2029, and was supplied to pharmacies in 1,000-count bottles and dispensed to patients in smaller quantities. If a client mentions they use generic acetaminophen for post-workout soreness or headaches, it is worth telling them to check that lot number against the bottle before their next dose.

One more, for anyone who wears a fitness tracker or coaches clients through one. Outside Online has a piece out on how skin tone affects wearable sensor accuracy, and how the major tech companies are responding to the problem. The core issue is that optical heart rate sensors, the kind built into most watches and rings, can read less reliably on darker skin because of how light reflects off different melanin levels. Outside reports the big wearable makers have been adjusting hardware and algorithms to close that gap. If you or a client leans on heart rate zones to guide training intensity, that is a real source of error worth factoring in rather than assuming the number on the wrist is exact.
talkingPoints: New Harvard study in the British Journal of Sports Medicine: 90 to 119 minutes of weekly lifting linked to 13% lower all-cause mortality over 30 years.
Same study found a 27% lower risk of dying from neurological disease, including dementia, in that lifting group.

blocks.label: Parenting
blocks.title: Child Benefit Jumps, Paediatric Sleep Rules Unchanged
blocks.script:
The biggest number for parents this fall comes from Ottawa. The Canada Child Benefit is going out with an increase, and starting this month it provides families with up to $8,157 per child under six and up to $6,883 per child aged six to 17. Households making less than $38,237 get the maximum benefit for each child with no reductions. Above that line, the benefit is clawed back gradually depending on income and number of children. If you're doing year end planning with young families, that threshold is worth flagging, because a bonus or a income-splitting decision can push a household across it and cost them real money.

On parental leave, the choice between standard Employment Insurance benefits at 55 percent of earnings for up to 40 weeks shared between parents, or the extended option at a lower weekly rate for up to 61 weeks, still shapes cash flow planning for a full year. It's a good prompt to revisit with any client expecting a baby.

On savings, the Registered Education Savings Plan grant is unchanged, 20 percent on the first 2,500 dollars contributed per child each year, an easy first conversation with new parents.

On health, the Canadian Paediatric Society's safe sleep guidance hasn't moved: back to sleep every time, a firm flat surface, room sharing for six months, nothing soft in the crib. Before four months, frequent night waking is biologically normal, and the Society does not endorse sleep training before that age.

On screens, for children under two, the Society still recommends screen time be avoided, with roughly an hour a day allowed from two to five.

None of your watch list names turned up in today's parenting research.
talkingPoints: The Canada Child Benefit rose again this year, worth checking against your clients' family income planning.
Households under about $38,000 in net income get the full benefit, above that it phases down.
The RESP grant is still 20 percent on the first 2,500 dollars a year per child.
EI parental leave choice, standard versus extended, changes a family's cash flow for over a year.
Paediatric guidance still says no sleep training before four months and no screens before age two.

blocks.label: Sports
blocks.title: Seahawks Stun Patriots as NFL Season Opens
blocks.script:
Good evening. We start with football, where the NFL season opener delivered plenty of drama. The Seattle Seahawks beat the New England Patriots 13-10 in a rematch of last year's Super Bowl, according to The Athletic's newsletter coverage. Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold left the game with a hip injury on the first series, and the Globe and Mail reports doctors found no broken bones or fractures, though his status going forward remains uncertain. Backup Drew Lock came in and led two scoring drives late, including a 45-yard touchdown pass, to help Seattle come from behind.

On the other side, Patriots quarterback Drake Maye had a chance to win it in the final minute but threw an interception that sealed New England's 0-1 start, per The Athletic. Patriots receiver A.J. Brown also left with an ankle injury in the third quarter.

The NFL's international slate continued in Australia, where the San Francisco 49ers routed the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 in the league's first game held down under, the Globe and Mail reports. The contest drew a crowd of just over 100,000, one of the largest in NFL regular season history. The Athletic noted the two teams took very different approaches to the trip, with San Francisco arriving a week early and Los Angeles landing just two days before kickoff.

Elsewhere in the NFL, Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs pleaded no contest to two misdemeanor charges, including battery, according to the Globe and Mail, and the league says it is monitoring the case for possible discipline.

In hockey, the sport lost one of its most familiar broadcast voices. Barry Melrose, the former NHL coach and longtime ESPN analyst, died Wednesday at age 70, his wife confirmed to ESPN, as reported by The Athletic. Melrose had retired in 2023 following a Parkinson's disease diagnosis and spent decades as one of the sport's most recognizable television personalities.

Closer to home, the Edmonton Oilers are facing intense backlash after signing forward Alex Formenton, one of five players from Canada's 2018 world junior team who were accused of sexual assault before being acquitted last year, according to CBC Sports and the Globe and Mail. The team's superfan known as "Mama Stanley" has withdrawn her support over the signing.

In baseball, the Los Angeles Dodgers placed four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani on the injured list, manager Dave Roberts confirmed, according to The Athletic. The move ends a months-long saga over his nagging injuries and opens a roster spot for top prospect Josue De Paula.

On the international stage, Canada's women's wheelchair basketball team improved to 2-0 at the world championships in Ottawa, defeating Australia 79-30 behind 33 points from Kady Dandeneau, per the Globe and Mail and CBC Sports. Canadian cyclist Michael Woods is also coming out of retirement to race for the national team at the road cycling world championships in Montreal, CBC Sports reports.

ers dominate Rams in NFL's historic first game in Australia.
